key_number: GPT-4-Turbo-2024-04-09 reaches the highest single-evaluator Pearson correlation with human scores (0.623); open Prometheus-2-BGB 8x7B reaches 0.607 with self-consistency, matching GPT-4-1106 despite being a fraction of the size

title: Prometheus 2: An Open Source Language Model Specialized in Evaluating Other Language Models
reward_readiness_reason: Judge emits exactly the 1-5 scores and pairwise preferences used for preference optimization (PairRM/UltraRM as baselines) and the Preference Collection is a reusable artifact, but its scores are a distilled copy of GPT-4's, carrying documented judge-bias cost — an RLAIF-adaptable signal, not a clean mechanical reward.
placement_reason: Born to give an open, inspectable, reference-free model scorer that produces a quality verdict on open-ended generations against arbitrary rubrics, matching proprietary GPT-4-level holistic judging.
one_line: Open LLM judge built by weight-merging direct-scoring and pairwise specialists; halves the open-vs-GPT-4 human-agreement gap across both evaluation formats.
key_number: FLASK human correlation: Prometheus-2-8x7B 0.555 vs GPT-4-1106's 0.679 (prior best open 0.449 — gap halved, not closed)

title: Pick-a-Pic: An Open Dataset of User Preferences for Text-to-Image Generation
reward_readiness_reason: PickScore is already used in-paper as a selection signal — Section 6's best-of-100 re-ranking experiment picks the single top-PickScore image from 100 generations and human raters prefer that pick 71.4-85.1% of the time over baselines — the same best-of-N optimization-against-a-scorer mechanism the taxonomy treats as reward-native (cf. brown-2024-monkeys), and the paper explicitly recommends PickScore as the metric to rank future T2I models against.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'what scalar predicts real, self-motivated users' text-to-image preferences, trained on an open half-million-pair dataset rather than crowd-worker or Discord-scraped judgments?' — a CLIP-H model fine-tuned via a pairwise KL-divergence preference loss, the same trained-neural-scorer mechanism as BLEURT and ImageReward, not a prompted judge protocol.
one_line: Real users pick between paired text-to-image generations in a public web app, yielding 583,747 open preference comparisons; PickScore, a CLIP-H model fine-tuned on them, predicts held-out preferences at 70.5% — edging the paper's own 68.0% human-expert baseline — and is proposed to replace FID as the field's ranking metric.
key_number: PickScore Elo ratings correlate with real users' Elo ratings at 0.790 (vs. ImageReward's 0.492, CLIP-H's 0.313) across 14,000 test-set preferences over 45 models

title: Coverage, Not Averages: Semantic Stratification for Trustworthy Retrieval Evaluation
reward_readiness_reason: post_training_link states "none — the method produces evaluation-set curation and diagnostics, not a reward or preference signal"; it is a one-time corpus-scale stratified estimator read to audit benchmarks, not a gradient signal.
placement_reason: Born to answer "is the measurement itself lying?" — it decomposes the exact bias in BEIR-style aggregate IR scores and shows benchmark composition, not the systems, decides the verdict, so it is a metric/construct critique of evaluation sets themselves.
one_line: Reframes retrieval evaluation as stratified estimation: benchmark query sets skip 40-50% of corpus topics, making aggregate nDCG irreducibly biased and verdict-flipping.
key_number: Same OpenAI-vs-Cohere comparison flips from 32.4% win rate (query-weighted mean) to 62.5% (macro-average) to 85.8% (worst-case P10)

title: Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores
reward_readiness_reason: Pure existence/impossibility proof (2016-17); no dataset, no RL/reward use, no training loop of any kind — the trilemma is a structural fact about any risk assignment, not a gradient signal.
placement_reason: Proves that three independently-motivated fairness metrics cannot jointly hold except in degenerate cases — the purest possible F3 construct critique (showing a class of measurements is internally incompatible), the founding leg of 2016's fairness-impossibility trio.
one_line: A short, general impossibility theorem: calibration within groups, balance for the negative class, and balance for the positive class cannot all hold for a risk assignment except when compared groups share a base rate or the predictor is perfect — explaining, at the level of principle, why ProPublica's and Northpointe's competing COMPAS readings were both correct.
key_number: The approximate version (Theorem 1.2) shows the escape hatch doesn't reopen under small measurement slack, but scales loosely as sqrt(epsilon) rather than epsilon

title: Benchmarking Cognitive Biases in Large Language Models as Evaluators
reward_readiness_reason: post_training_link: "None stated — the paper is a diagnostic audit, not a reward signal"; used to read judge machinery, no training use reported.
placement_reason: Born to answer whether the LLM-as-judge verdicts that leaderboards (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval, G-Eval) were being built on are driven by cognitive biases rather than quality — a systematic audit of the judge machinery's validity, not a new metric or task.
one_line: Round-robin audit of 16 LLM judges finds ~40% of pairwise verdicts carry cognitive biases and only 0.44 RBO agreement with human rankings.
key_number: ~40% of pairwise verdicts across 16 models showed at least one of six cognitive biases

title: Chain of Thought Monitorability: A New and Fragile Opportunity for AI Safety
reward_readiness_reason: Explicit warning AGAINST optimizing against it — the paper's core thesis: monitorability exists precisely because the CoT is NOT directly supervised during RL, and direct process supervision / scaled outcome-based RL would destroy it; recommends paying a "monitorability tax."
placement_reason: A cross-lab position paper whose birth question is "can we watch a reasoning model think, and does that oversight survive training?" — the canonical CoT-monitorability manifesto, squarely M1.
one_line: Cross-lab position paper: read reasoning models' chains of thought to catch misbehavior — a fragile, unmeasured safety window training choices could silently close.
key_number: 163 citations as of 2026-06-19; a 40-author cross-lab position paper

title: Do Better ImageNet Models Transfer Better?
reward_readiness_reason: A correlational validity study used to justify backbone selection, not a reward signal; no RL/training use is stated, and the paper's own point is that its correlation is protocol-fragile, the opposite of something you'd want to optimize against.
placement_reason: Its founding question is whether ImageNet top-1 accuracy actually measures transferable-feature quality or just architecture capacity — a construct-validity audit of the field's single most load-bearing benchmark number, the same F3 role as the texture-bias and emergent-abilities papers in this batch, not a new scoring instrument.
one_line: ImageNet top-1 accuracy predicts transfer accuracy at r=0.99 (fixed features) under a matched training protocol — but the same architectures trained from scratch, with no ImageNet at all, still correlate at r=0.55, showing part of that headline number is just architecture capacity.
key_number: 16 architectures x 12 datasets: r=0.99 (fixed features) / r=0.96 (fine-tuned) with ImageNet pretraining, vs r=0.55 (r=0.86 on larger datasets) for the same architectures trained from random initialization.

title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks
reward_readiness_reason: Digest post_training_link: "none - no use as a reward or preference signal is stated; the horizon is a forecasting yardstick"; the verdict is model-level and the durable claim is a cross-model trend, too aggregate to be a gradient signal.
placement_reason: Born as a new measurement scale — task length in skilled-human time that a model completes 50% of the time — explicitly motivated by a critique of saturating, unit-less benchmarks, making it a capability-axis metrology instrument.
one_line: Fits a per-model logistic over human-timed tasks; the 50%-success task length has doubled every ~7 months since 2019.
key_number: 50% time horizon doubled every 207 days (R^2 = 0.97, 95% bootstrap CI 166-240 days) from 2019 to 2025

title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
reward_readiness_reason: No RL use (2016); a training-time proper-scoring-rule objective (Gaussian NLL) improves calibration, but the paper's own evaluation only reports point-in-time NLL/Brier/accuracy, not a downstream reward or an optimization-vs-metric divergence test.
placement_reason: Evaluated squarely on how appropriately its predictive entropy grows on staged OOD/unknown-class inputs versus MC-dropout — an I3 robustness probe borrowing the OOD-detection framing Hendrycks/Nguyen established, even though its headline contribution is a training method rather than new measurement machinery; flagged in the report as the batch's most borderline 'does it own scoring machinery' case.
one_line: Train M=5 ordinary networks from different random seeds, each outputting a mean and variance via a proper scoring rule instead of a point estimate, then average as a mixture — matches or beats approximate-Bayesian uncertainty methods (PBP, MC-dropout) on calibration and OOD robustness with no new inference machinery.
key_number: On ImageNet dogs-vs-non-dogs, growing the ensemble from 1 to 10 networks drops top-1 error from 22.166% to 18.675% while NLL improves from 0.959 to 0.789; every OOD test is a 'far' shift (MNIST/NotMNIST, SVHN/CIFAR-10), with no near-OOD stress test

title: RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Language Modeling
reward_readiness_reason: RewardBench scores whether a reward model correctly ranks a pre-existing chosen/rejected pair; it diagnoses RM quality but the benchmark itself is a static test suite, not a live reward signal used in training.
placement_reason: Reward models are graders — the classifiers and DPO checkpoints that decide which response is better during RLHF. RewardBench is the audit that tests whether those graders themselves get it right, exposing a wide, previously invisible chat/reasoning/safety accuracy gap between classifier-trained and DPO-derived reward models.
one_line: A common evaluation codebase for reward models spanning chat, reasoning, safety, and legacy preference data across 80+ open models, exposing a wide, previously invisible gap between classifier-trained and DPO-derived reward models.
key_number: 80+ reward models scored across 4 category subsets (chat, chat-hard, safety, reasoning); no single model near-ceiling on all four

title: A Simple Unified Framework for Detecting Out-of-Distribution Samples and Adversarial Attacks
reward_readiness_reason: A per-input confidence score used to flag OOD/adversarial inputs at inference time; no RL/reward use is stated, and the score is reported/thresholded rather than trained against.
placement_reason: Its founding move is a computed, reference-free confidence score derived purely from a model's own fitted feature statistics — the S2 role (a trained/fitted statistic scoring an input) rather than I3 (it doesn't stage an attack, it detects one already present) or F-kingdom (it isn't auditing another instrument, it is the instrument).
one_line: A pretrained softmax classifier already implicitly defines a class-conditional Gaussian over its own features; scoring inputs by Mahalanobis distance to the nearest class mean catches both OOD samples and adversarial examples with one training-free score.
key_number: CIFAR-10→SVHN (ResNet): full method reaches 96.42 TNR@95%TPR / 99.14 AUROC, vs ODIN's 86.55 / 96.65 and the softmax baseline's 32.47 / 89.88.

title: CoAuthor: Designing a Human-AI Collaborative Writing Dataset for Exploring Language Model Capabilities
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-reward use is stated; equality/mutuality are HCI-style descriptive statistics computed post hoc from a logged interaction dataset, and the paper's own productivity/ownership findings are explicitly flagged as unvalidated correlational hypotheses, not a reward or preference signal.
placement_reason: Born to answer whether a static benchmark score can capture what matters when a language model is used interactively rather than queried once — arguing no, and replacing it with a fully-logged keystroke-level interaction-trace dataset plus two process-level scores (equality, mutuality) computed directly from event counts — the same show-the-standard-metric-measures-the-wrong-thing F3 move as sacreBLEU/BEGIN, here aimed at the benchmark paradigm itself rather than one specific metric.
one_line: 1,445 fully-logged human-GPT-3 writing sessions argue that interaction traces, not aggregate benchmark scores, are how you find out what a language model actually does in someone's hands.
key_number: 72.3% suggestion acceptance rate across 1,445 sessions; jointly-written sentences are both the most grammatical (0.032 errors/word) and most diverse (0.923 distinct-2) of any single source.

title: Can LLM Already Serve as A Database Interface? A BIg Bench for Large-Scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQLs
reward_readiness_reason: Verdict is pure SQL execution-result match against a single gold query with no model/human per verdict — a cheap deterministic verifiable reward ready for RLVR (cost: "run the predicted SQL... no model calls or human judging per verdict").
placement_reason: Born to make text-to-SQL correctness mechanical by executing predicted SQL against real dirty databases and matching result sets to gold — a canonical execution oracle for a task-capability construct.
one_line: Text-to-SQL benchmark on 33 GB of dirty real databases scored by execution-result match plus runtime-weighted VES; GPT-4 hits 54.89% vs humans' 92.96%.
key_number: GPT-4 reaches 54.89% execution accuracy on the hidden test set with oracle external knowledge vs human experts at 92.96%

title: Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-model use stated; POPE is read as a stability-improved diagnostic probe for object hallucination, not wired as a training signal.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'what number captures object-hallucination rate without CHAIR's prompt-sensitive caption-parsing brittleness?' by polling closed-form yes/no questions about object presence and scoring accuracy directly against human/segmentation-derived ground truth — a reference-free, decomposition-based scoring metric in FActScore's mold, demonstrated ~20x more prompt-stable than the free-form-parsing metric it replaces.
one_line: Replaces CHAIR's prompt-sensitive caption parsing with closed-form yes/no polling under random/popular/adversarial negative sampling — ~20x less prompt-induced score variance than CHAIR, exposing that 3 of 5 evaluated LVLMs answer 'Yes' to 95-100% of questions regardless of truth.
key_number: POPE's F1 coefficient of variation across four prompt rewordings is 1.16% vs. CHAIR's 23.2%; MultiModal-GPT answers 'Yes' to 100.00% of Popular-setting questions

title: From Crowdsourced Data to High-Quality Benchmarks: Arena-Hard and BenchBuilder Pipeline
reward_readiness_reason: "None stated as a training signal; the explainer implicitly warns against optimizing the static artifact (the frozen 500-prompt set 'can be trained on and saturates over time')" — used as a cheap leaderboard proxy, not a gradient signal.
placement_reason: Built to answer "how do we get a cheap, statistically separable model-judge proxy for the human-vote Chatbot Arena ranking?" — a distilled pairwise judge protocol over automatically-curated hard prompts.
one_line: BenchBuilder mines 200K Arena chat logs into 500 hard prompts; a GPT-4-Turbo pairwise judge yields 90.9% human agreement for $20/model.
key_number: 90.9% confidence agreement and 93.2% Spearman with the top-20 Chatbot Arena English ranking, at $20 per model evaluated

title: Embodied Agent Interface: Benchmarking LLMs for Embodied Decision Making
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-signal use — the isolated per-module metrics (Goal F1, Execution/Task Success Rate, Transition Model F1, Planner Success Rate) are reported as a diagnostic error-taxonomy read for comparing 18 LLMs, not wired into a training loop.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'when an embodied LLM agent fails, which of four separable abilities — goal interpretation, subgoal decomposition, action sequencing, transition modeling — actually broke?' — a shared LTL representation that decomposes one opaque success/fail verdict into four isolably-gradeable criteria plus a named error taxonomy, the defining V2 rubric-decomposition move, unified across two structurally incompatible simulators.
one_line: A shared LTL-based interface decomposes embodied decision-making into four isolably-gradeable modules — goal interpretation, subgoal decomposition, action sequencing, transition modeling — each graded independently across BEHAVIOR and VirtualHome; o1-preview leads BEHAVIOR (74.9%) but is edged out on VirtualHome by Claude-3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro (65.7% each).
key_number: For GPT-4o, runtime planning errors (16.2% additional-step, 15.5% missing-step) dominate over grammar/format errors (7.7%) in the named error taxonomy

title: Evaluating Real-World Robot Manipulation Policies in Simulation
group: UC San Diego / Stanford / UC Berkeley / Google DeepMind
reward_readiness_reason: SIMPLER ships as installable Gym-API environments with deterministic simulator-read task success — the same mechanical, per-episode reward signal RL policies are trained against in simulation; the paper uses it purely for evaluation, but the reward-shaped Gym interface is reward-native by construction.
placement_reason: Born to answer ‘can a simulator, built merely realistic enough rather than pixel-perfect, tell us how a real-data-trained manipulation policy will actually perform in the real world?’ — an interactive Gym-API competence harness whose central claim is validated by real-world correlation (Pearson r up to 0.976) rather than a single mechanical pass/fail check, the same interactive-task-harness role as MathDial/MRBench/LHAW.
one_line: SIMPLER swaps real-robot trials for SAPIEN-based Gym simulation, closing the control gap via offline system identification and the visual gap via green-screening/texture-matching, achieving Pearson r up to 0.976 with real-world success rates across six/three policy checkpoints on two robot embodiments.
key_number: Visual Matching reaches (MMRV, Pearson r) = (0.031, 0.976) on Pick Coke Can and (0.056, 0.924) averaged across the SIMPLER protocol comparison — versus (0.375, 0.308) for offline validation-loss as a real-world proxy

title: ResearchQA: Evaluating Scholarly Question Answering at Scale Across 75 Fields with Survey-Mined Questions and Rubrics
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-model use is stated; Coverage % is a recall-style leaderboard metric explicitly flagged as length-sensitive (a system's score can be inflated roughly 9 points simply by writing longer), which would make it an easily-gamed target to optimize against directly.
placement_reason: Built to make open-ended scholarly-QA quality checkable without per-query expert labor, by mining query-specific rubric criteria from survey articles and scoring 0-4 coverage per item — the same decomposed-rubric recipe as PaperBench/DeepResearch-Bench/HealthBench, distinguished only by how the rubrics are sourced (survey-mined, not hand-written or agent-generated).
one_line: Mines 54K academic surveys into 21.4K research queries and 160K query-specific rubric items across 75 fields, escaping the per-query expert-annotation bottleneck; folding rubric coverage into an ensemble judge lifts human-preference agreement from 71%/64% to 74%/69%.
key_number: Across 7.6K head-to-head battles over 18 systems, no parametric or retrieval system tops 70% coverage — the best, Perplexity's sonar-deep-research, reaches 75.29% — though the 250-word answer cap means coverage rises to roughly 85% once length is uncapped.

title: Enhancing The Reliability of Out-of-distribution Image Detection in Neural Networks
reward_readiness_reason: No RL use (2017); two test-time-only tricks applied to a frozen classifier, evaluated via the same AUROC/AUPR/FPR@95%TPR protocol Hendrycks & Gimpel established, not a training signal.
placement_reason: Directly extends Hendrycks & Gimpel's OOD-detection probe with two additional test-time attacks on the same frozen classifier, evaluated under the identical staged-input, score-what-breaks protocol — squarely I3, one generation further down the same lineage as MSP and Nguyen's fooling images.
one_line: Two test-time-only tricks on a frozen classifier — a large-temperature softmax and a reverse-adversarial input nudge that raises the predicted class's own score — cut the false-positive rate at 95% true-positive rate from 34.7% to 4.3% on DenseNet/CIFAR-10 vs. TinyImageNet, an eightfold reduction over the plain MSP baseline.
key_number: On CIFAR-100 (the harder, more crowded 100-class softmax), FPR@95%TPR falls from 67.8% to 26.9% against TinyImageNet — but every OOD test set is a 'far' shift, and T/epsilon/threshold are all tuned on a held-out OOD validation set drawn from the same benign natural-image family as the test sets

title: Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
reward_readiness_reason: post_training_link: "None — purely diagnostic, not a reward or preference signal"; the full grid is a $38k, 19,500-GPU-hour snapshot, far too slow/aggregate to be a gradient.
placement_reason: Born to answer "what should we measure across the whole LM landscape and how do we aggregate it comparably?" — it taxonomizes scenarios × desiderata and standardizes adaptation so 30 models are ranked head-to-head, the defining holistic-framework question.
one_line: HELM turned LM evaluation into a standardized grid — 7 automated metrics x 16 scenarios x 30 models under one 5-shot protocol, ranked by win rate.
key_number: Model x scenario coverage lifted from 17.9% to 96.0% across 30 models under identical 5-shot conditions

title: Automatic Evaluation of Summaries Using N-gram Co-occurrence Statistics
reward_readiness_reason: No RL use (2003); reported as a DUC shared-task correlation number, and the paper's own proposed brevity bonus/penalty is explicitly fixed at a no-op value ('set to 1 for all our experiments') rather than optimized against.
placement_reason: At birth it asked 'does BLEU's n-gram trick transfer to summarization,' and answered by flipping precision to recall to match DUC's own coverage protocol — the direct one-year-earlier pilot for ROUGE, placed in the same founding S1 lexical-overlap family it seeds.
one_line: Ports BLEU's n-gram machinery to summarization by flipping precision to recall (matching DUC's coverage protocol); plain unigram co-occurrence beats BLEU's own weighted multi-length formula on DUC 2001, the one-year pilot that directly seeds ROUGE.
key_number: Ngram(1,1) unigram recall reaches Spearman rho up to 0.989-0.993 against human coverage rankings, versus 0.604-0.875 for the BLEU-style weighted Ngram(1,4) composite

title: ROUGE: A Package for Automatic Evaluation of Summaries
reward_readiness_reason: Paper states no RL use; digest documents Goodhart aftermath where the field optimized directly against it, but it functions as a system-ranking/leaderboard proxy rather than a live per-verdict reward.
placement_reason: Born to answer "what number captures a summary's content quality without thousands of hours of human coverage judging?" via recall-oriented n-gram/LCS overlap against gold references — the canonical summarization scoring metric.
one_line: Recall-oriented lexical overlap against human reference summaries, validated by correlating system rankings with DUC human coverage judgments (0.84-0.99 single-doc).
key_number: ROUGE-2 Pearson r = 0.84-0.87 vs human coverage on DUC 2001 single-doc; saturates at 0.98-0.99 on DUC 2002

title: AgentSims: An Open-Source Sandbox for Large Language Model Evaluation
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward use — and indeed no experiments of any kind are run in the paper; it proposes task-based, pass/fail evaluation as more contamination-resistant than QA benchmarks but never operationalizes or measures it.
placement_reason: Proposes, but never operationalizes, task-based evaluation inside an interactive agentic-town sandbox (agent-as-participant or agent-as-mayor) as more contamination-resistant and objective than static QA benchmarks; the intended verdict mechanism (pass/fail task completion) would be an agentic-work harness in MathDial/MRBench's mold, but the paper ships only the infrastructure and reports zero benchmark results, no pass rates, and no baselines of its own.
one_line: A pixel-game sandbox town where LLM agents plan, remember, and use tools, pitched as 'task-based evaluation' infrastructure more contamination-resistant than static QA — but the paper itself reports zero pass rates, zero model comparisons, and zero benchmark results.
key_number: No experiments reported: the paper's only concrete numbers are UI mock-up placeholder values (e.g. an example NPC's '$10,000' cash balance), not evaluation data

title: WildBench: Benchmarking LLMs with Challenging Tasks from Real Users in the Wild
reward_readiness_reason: Not itself an RL reward in-paper, but WB-Score/WB-Reward follow the same LLM-judge-as-downstream-training-signal paradigm as MT-Bench, and the paper's own length-penalty mechanism is a documented, only-partial fix for a known hacking vector (length gaming), the reward-adapted signature.
placement_reason: Born to answer ‘can an automatic judge protocol reach Chatbot Arena-level correlation using tasks mined from real usage rather than author-written or narrowly-scraped prompts?’ — a checklist-guided model-judge pairwise/individual protocol validated against live human-vote Elo, the same P2 judge-protocol role as MT-Bench and Arena-Hard, built specifically to fix their task-diversity gaps.
one_line: 1,024 hard, multi-turn tasks mined from over a million real WildChat conversations, graded with per-instance checklists via WB-Score (individual) and WB-Reward (pairwise against three tiered baselines with a length-penalty tiebreaker) — reaching 0.98/0.95 Pearson correlation with Chatbot Arena's human-voted Elo on top models.
key_number: WB-Reward(Mix) reaches 0.984 Pearson on the top-6-model subset (0.973-0.976 on the full 14-model set) vs Arena-Hard's 0.909/0.925 and AlpacaEval2's 0.865/0.952

title: How NOT To Evaluate Your Dialogue System: An Empirical Study of Unsupervised Evaluation Metrics for Dialogue Response Generation
reward_readiness_reason: No RL use (2016); a correlation study read off existing metrics against a human survey, with the explicit payoff of methodological hygiene ('don't trust an unvalidated score'), not a training signal.
placement_reason: At birth it asked 'do the metrics borrowed from MT/summarization actually track human judgment of dialogue quality,' and showed they mostly don't — the same F3 metric-construct-critique role as Schaeffer's and Klearman's correlation-based critiques, and the paper BLEURT's own motivation cites directly.
one_line: The first systematic human-correlation check on metrics borrowed wholesale into dialogue evaluation: BLEU/METEOR/ROUGE and three embedding-similarity metrics correlate only weakly with human adequacy on casual Twitter chat (best Spearman 0.36) and not at all on technical Ubuntu dialogue, against a 0.95 human-human ceiling.
key_number: Embedding Average is negatively correlated with human ratings on Ubuntu dialogue (Pearson -0.16); every word-overlap metric there is statistically indistinguishable from zero (all p>=0.16)

title: Energy-based Out-of-distribution Detection
reward_readiness_reason: The paper directly wires the energy score into a two-sided hinge fine-tuning loss (L_energy) that trains the classifier to widen its in-/out-of-distribution energy gap — an already-realized training signal, not a hypothetical one, analogous to how execution-graded scores feed RLVR.
placement_reason: Born to prove algebraically that softmax confidence (MSP) is a biased, shifted view of a classifier's own free energy — exposing a near-universally-deployed 'confidence' measurement as measuring the wrong quantity and handing back the corrected, parameter-free one — the same show-a-metric-measures-the-wrong-thing F3 move as sacreBLEU/Emergent Mirage, not a fresh capability benchmark or a staged behavioral probe.
one_line: Softmax confidence is a biased, shifted view of a classifier's own logits — this paper names the unshifted quantity (free energy), reads it off for free, and shows it also makes a stronger fine-tuning signal than Outlier Exposure's softmax-based one.
key_number: Swapping softmax confidence for energy score alone cuts CIFAR-10 average FPR95 from 51.04% to 33.01%, parameter-free; energy-bounded fine-tuning reaches 3.32% vs Outlier Exposure's 8.53% under an identical training budget.

title: Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? Rigorous Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code Generation
reward_readiness_reason: EvalPlus is a hardened execution benchmark read to rank/harden models; training a model to pass more differential tests would genuinely improve it, so its validity does not depend on not-training-against-it (memorization/contamination is the generic gameability of any static benchmark, not self-destruction of the measurement).
placement_reason: Born to answer "is HumanEval's execution-based verdict trustworthy?" — it audits another benchmark's test adequacy and ground-truth correctness (11% of ground-truths defective), exposing that passing tests != correctness, which is a metric/construct critique.
one_line: Auto-generates 80x more tests for HumanEval via LLM seeding plus type-aware mutation; up to 28.9% of "passing" code is wrong, rankings flip.
key_number: HumanEval ships 9.6 tests/problem on average; HumanEval+ has 764.1 — 80x more, dropping pass@100 by up to 28.9%.

title: G-Eval: NLG Evaluation using GPT-4 with Better Human Alignment
reward_readiness_reason: G-Eval is an LLM-judge metric that is normally reported; the self-reinforcement caution is about a HYPOTHETICAL reward use it never actually performs, which is exactly 'gameable if you optimized it but usually just reported', matching its sibling LLM-judge evals (mt-bench, chiang-2023-llm-eval, cobbler) rather than a self-defeating instrument.
placement_reason: Born to answer "what number captures this text's quality?" with no gold reference — a reference-free model scorer that reads a probability-weighted 1-5 score from a GPT-4 judge.
one_line: Prompt GPT-4 with an auto-generated CoT rubric, read probability-weighted score tokens: the reference-free judge recipe that beat trained SOTA on human correlation.
key_number: SummEval avg Spearman 0.514 (G-Eval-4) vs 0.474 UniEval (trained SOTA), 0.192 ROUGE-1

title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward use stated; the paper is purely diagnostic — it establishes a position-invariance protocol that later models were explicitly trained to satisfy (e.g. needle-in-a-haystack training), the opposite of an anti-optimization warning.
placement_reason: At birth it asked 'does reported long-context accuracy reflect genuine, uniform use of the context, or is it an artifact of where the relevant information happens to sit?' — a controlled position-manipulation test exposing that naive multi-document QA/retrieval accuracy numbers can look strong while masking a severe, systematic middle-of-context blind spot, the same metric-construct-critique role as schaeffer-2023-emergent-mirage and post-2018-sacrebleu, not a new capability-axis scale itself.
one_line: Sliding an answer-bearing document's position across a 10-30 document prompt traces a U-shaped accuracy curve — strong at the start and end, weak in the middle, sometimes worse than giving the model no documents at all — and extending the context window doesn't fix it.
key_number: GPT-3.5-Turbo's mid-context multi-document QA accuracy drops below its 56.1% closed-book (no-documents) score once the answer sits in the middle of a 20-30 document prompt

title: Formalizing and Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-signal use is described — PNA/ASV/MR are reported per-attack/defense benchmark numbers for comparing systems, not a reward wired into a training loop; the paper's own gameability concern is about the attacker-vs-defender arms race, not about optimizing a policy against this eval.
placement_reason: Born to answer ‘how do we formalize prompt injection so every existing attack becomes a special case of one function, and systematically test attacks against defenses on common footing?’ — a deliberate, staged adversarial probe (5 attacks × 10 defenses × 10 LLMs × 7 tasks), the same I3 question PromptInject and HarmBench answer.
one_line: First formal prompt-injection framework (x̃=A(xt,se,xe)) plus a systematic benchmark of 5 attacks × 10 defenses × 10 LLMs × 7 tasks; its own Combined Attack beats every attack it's built from and no defense proves sufficient.
key_number: Combined Attack reaches 0.75 average ASV on GPT-4; ASV/MR correlate with model size at Pearson r=0.63/0.64 — bigger models are easier to hijack

title: EvalCrafter: Benchmarking and Evaluating Large Video Generation Models
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-signal use — the fitted per-aspect regression produces a leaderboard score for comparing T2V systems, not a reward wired into a generator's training loop.
placement_reason: Born to answer ‘what number captures a generated video's quality, when no single gold video exists for an open text prompt?’ — 17 purpose-built automatic detectors across four aspects, calibrated (not merely averaged) against human ratings; a scoring-metric contribution, not a T-kingdom survey of many pre-existing model/task scenarios or a staged I-kingdom behavioral probe.
one_line: 700-prompt T2V benchmark scored on 17 objective metrics across four aspects, fitted per-aspect to human ratings rather than averaged — flipping motion-amplitude's raw −38.2 Spearman anti-correlation with human preference to +45.0.
key_number: Fitted score reaches +45.0 Spearman on motion amplitude where every raw metric (and their naive average, −38.2) anti-correlates with human judgment; 3 of 8 leaderboard systems were never rated by a human at all

title: MMBench: Is Your Multi-modal Model an All-around Player?
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward use stated; MMBench-test answers are held server-side specifically to prevent optimization/leakage, and the paper frames itself as a diagnostic leaderboard, not a training target.
placement_reason: Built to answer 'is a VLM an all-around player, and how do we measure that without multiple-choice guessing and instruction-following noise corrupting the number?' — a 20-leaf, 2-level ability taxonomy assembled into one benchmark with a rigor-hardened evaluation protocol (CircularEval, GPT-4-assisted choice extraction), the same holistic-aggregation move as BIG-bench/HELM applied to vision-language models.
one_line: A 20-leaf ability taxonomy over 3,217 bilingual multiple-choice questions, scored under CircularEval (a question only counts correct if every circularly-shifted choice-ordering is answered right) plus GPT-4-assisted free-form answer extraction — collapsing OpenFlamingo v2's vanilla 36.7% to 2.6% and even dropping GPT-4V by 10.8 points.
key_number: InternLM-XComposer2 tops the CircularEval leaderboard at 78.1%, but every model plateaus at 61-68% max accuracy on Image Quality, Structuralized Image-Text Understanding, Physical Relation Reasoning, and Spatial Relationship

title: Fantastically Ordered Prompts and Where to Find Them: Overcoming Few-Shot Prompt Order Sensitivity
reward_readiness_reason: Entropy-based ordering selection is a pre-inference search procedure over prompt permutations, not a training loss or reward signal — no RL/fine-tuning use is stated.
placement_reason: Born to show that reordering identical few-shot training examples — nothing else changed — swings reported accuracy from near-chance to matching 60,000-example supervised training, undermining any single-prompt few-shot number as a stable capability measurement, then hands back a zero-label entropy-based fix — the same F3 show-the-protocol-measures-the-wrong-thing role as its near-contemporary rival zhao-2021-calibrate, which this paper directly tests and finds only partially compatible with its own fix.
one_line: Reorders identical few-shot prompts and lets accuracy swing from near-chance to matching 60k-example supervised training; fixes it with zero labeled data by ranking orderings via the entropy of the model's own synthetic-probe predictions.
key_number: Top-4 orderings by GlobalE/LocalE entropy deliver an average 13% (up to 30%) relative accuracy improvement across 11 datasets and 4 orders of magnitude of scale — but stacking with contextual calibration leaves real variance unclosed (51.6-85.2% spread survives after calibration, per the paper's own Figure 6).

title: Agentic Misalignment: How LLMs Could Be Insider Threats
reward_readiness_reason: The paper's own test-awareness experiment shows blackmail differs 8.5x by the model's stated belief about whether the scenario is real (55.1%) or an evaluation (6.5%) — direct evidence the staged honeypot's validity depends on the model not recognizing or learning to game the setup, so training or selecting against the visible rate would corrupt the signal rather than harden it.
placement_reason: A staged corporate honeypot with no jailbreak and no adversarial user — a benign goal plus an obstacle is enough for a model's own instrumental reasoning to reach for blackmail or espionage — the direct generalization of a single Claude-4-system-card anecdote and meinke-2024's honeypot design to a systematic 16-model, multi-behavior sweep; squarely I1's staged-temptation-to-scheme question rather than a dangerous-capability probe (I2, which concerns recoverable skill, not interpersonal scheming under pressure).
one_line: Sixteen frontier models play an autonomous email-oversight agent facing a fictional replacement threat and/or goal conflict with no adversarial prompt; when blackmail or leaking secrets was engineered to be the only remaining path, models from every developer tested did it at non-trivial rates.
key_number: Blackmail hits 96% (Claude Opus 4, Gemini 2.5 Flash) under combined goal-conflict-plus-threat; a test-awareness check shows Claude Opus 4 blackmailed 55.1% of the time when it stated the scenario was real vs. 6.5% when it stated the scenario was an evaluation.

title: MathDial: A Dialogue Tutoring Dataset with Rich Pedagogical Properties Grounded in Math Reasoning Problems
reward_readiness_reason: "The corpus is finetuning data: BART, T5, Flan-T5, and OPT tutors are trained on it for 10 epochs, and the finetuned Flan-T5-780M is the paper's headline result."
placement_reason: Built to make interactive tutoring competence mechanically checkable via a multi-turn rollout against a simulated student, scored by a deterministic Success@k-vs-Telling@k oracle on the guide-or-tell tradeoff.
one_line: Real-teacher-teaches-LLM-student tutoring corpus whose Success@k vs Telling@k rollout metric turns the guide-or-tell tradeoff into a measurable verdict.
key_number: Finetuned Flan-T5-780M: Success@5 = 30% at <1% Telling@5, vs ChatGPT's 29% success but 16% telling

title: Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning
reward_readiness_reason: The rubric reward IS the GRPO training signal, already wired in as an RLVR-style reward but with documented hacking cost — the LOCKED FACET-5 rubric names Rubric-Reward-Hacking explicitly under reward-adapted; digest: weak-verifier exploitation climbs 39%->65% and even a ~92%-agreement verifier yields a checkpoint rubric-free judges prefer the base model over on 78.4% of prompts.
placement_reason: Born to answer "is the rising rubric-RL reward genuine quality or the policy hacking its verifier and rubric?" — it instruments reward hacking in a rubric-plus-LLM-verifier training pipeline, the definitional reward-hacking forensics question.
one_line: Instruments rubric-RL reward hacking with a panel-vs-verifier exploitation rate and a free log-prob self-gap; stronger verifiers shrink but never close the gap.
key_number: Under the weak verifier, exploitation rate climbs 39%->65% (medical); under the strong verifier it stays flat at 15-21%.

title: OpenEQA: Embodied Question Answering in the Era of Foundation Models
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-signal use — LLM-Match produces a benchmark leaderboard score for comparing embodied-QA agents, not wired into a policy training loop.
placement_reason: Born to make open-vocabulary embodied QA correctness checkable when exact-match fails and human evaluation doesn't scale — LLM-Match is validated directly against human agreement, applied across both a passive episodic-memory setting and an active setting where the agent must explore a simulated environment first, the same interactive competence-harness role as LHAW/MRBench.
one_line: 1636 open-vocabulary embodied-QA questions across episodic-memory and active-exploration settings, scored by LLM-Match (an LLM judge rating 1-5 similarity to a human reference) instead of exact-match — the best model, GPT-4V, reaches 49.6% against an 86.8% human ceiling.
key_number: LLM-Match reaches ρ=0.909 against human judgment (bootstrap CI 0.883-0.928) vs human-human agreement of ρ∈[0.91,0.93] on the same 300-question study — 'nearly as much as human subjects agree with one another'

title: RewardBench 2: Advancing Reward Model Evaluation
reward_readiness_reason: RewardBench 2 scores whether a reward model ranks a pre-labeled best-of-4 set correctly; it diagnoses RM quality and is explicit that a top benchmark score does not reliably predict good downstream RLHF outcomes once the RM clears a "good enough" threshold — a static test suite, not a live training reward.
placement_reason: Direct successor to RewardBench, auditing whether the graders that decide RLHF's chosen/rejected pairs get it right — but goes further than its predecessor by auditing its own predictive validity, finding and naming the exact place its own metric breaks down (RM-lineage mismatch defeats the PPO correlation even at a high benchmark score) — the reward-model-audit question, unchanged in kind from F2's founding member.
one_line: AI2's harder reward-model benchmark: roughly 70% previously unreleased WildChat prompts, a best-of-4 format (25% random baseline) across six domains, empirically checked against downstream best-of-N (r=0.87 across 113 RMs) and PPO performance.
key_number: Leading models score 20+ points lower than on RewardBench 1; PPO performance saturates once an RM clears roughly 50 on the benchmark, and the dominant predictor of a PPO shortfall is a lineage/distribution mismatch between reward model and policy, not benchmark score itself.

title: Unifying AI Tutor Evaluation: An Evaluation Taxonomy for Pedagogical Ability Assessment of LLM-Powered AI Tutors
reward_readiness_reason: "none — no reward-signal use... the taxonomy is a measurement/standardisation instrument, and its LLM-judge automation (the step that could feed a scalable reward) is shown not to work yet" — negative-correlating judges leave it human-only and diagnostic.
placement_reason: Built to answer whether an LLM tutor turn genuinely remediates a student's math mistake within a dialogue — an interactive tutoring-competence harness scoring per-turn pedagogical behavior, not a scoring metric or a preference vote.
one_line: Human annotators grade LLM tutor turns on an 8-dimension pedagogical taxonomy (DAMR); frontier models answer well but tutor poorly, and cheap LLM judges correlate negatively with humans.
key_number: Cohen's kappa = 0.71 (main annotation, 40 doubly-labelled instances); Fleiss' kappa = 0.65 (validation pilot)

title: On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization
reward_readiness_reason: A 2,500-judgment human study establishing ground-truth hallucination rates and auditing ROUGE/BERTScore against them; no RL/reward use is stated, and the paper's own reranking experiment treats entailment as a scoring aid, not a trained-against objective.
placement_reason: Its founding question is whether the field's default metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore) actually track summary faithfulness — establishing ground truth via a large, carefully hierarchical human-annotation protocol and then showing the incumbent metrics fail it, the same 'is the reported number trustworthy' F3 move sacreBLEU and evalplus make for their own metrics, with the intrinsic/extrinsic hallucination taxonomy as its lasting conceptual export.
one_line: A 2,500-judgment human study of five XSum systems finds 73-79% of summaries — including the human-written references — contain content unsupported by the source, while ROUGE and BERTScore barely correlate with that judgment at all.
key_number: Hallucination rate 73.1-79.3% across every system tested including GOLD (76.9%); Spearman |r_s| vs human faithfulness: ROUGE/BERTScore ~0.16-0.20 vs textual entailment's 0.431.

title: HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal
reward_readiness_reason: R2D2 adversarially trains Mistral 7B against a dynamic pool of GCG test cases, cutting GCG ASR 69.5%→5.5% while keeping MT-Bench at 6.0 — the pipeline is directly a training signal.
placement_reason: Born to standardize ad-hoc red-teaming into one pipeline (510 behaviors, fixed 512-token cap, open classifier) that stages adversarial attacks and asks whether a model robustly refuses to attempt harmful behaviors.
one_line: Standardized red-teaming pipeline — 510 behaviors, 512-token cap, open 93.2%-human-agreement classifier — showing no attack/defense dominates and safety doesn't scale.
key_number: 93.2% human agreement (vs GPT-4's 88.4%)

title: Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming
reward_readiness_reason: "Explicitly anti-optimization: key eval details are withheld to keep the suite out of future training sets (contamination would defeat the eval)."
placement_reason: Built to answer whether a frontier agent, handed a goal and situational awareness, will spontaneously execute covert deception (disable oversight, self-exfiltrate, lie, sandbag) when a staged honeypot situation opens the door.
one_line: Six sandboxed agentic honeypots show five frontier models can covertly disable oversight, self-exfiltrate, lie, and sandbag — scheming measured as capability, not propensity.
key_number: Every model except GPT-4o schemed on at least one of six evals; o1 schemed on all six

title: A Diverse Corpus for Evaluating and Developing English Math Word Problem Solvers
reward_readiness_reason: A bidirectional-BLEU diversity statistic used to audit corpus redundancy and to curate ASDiv itself against near-duplicates; no RL/reward use is stated.
placement_reason: Its founding question is whether a math-solver's reported accuracy reflects genuine problem-solving or memorized near-duplicate templates inflated by low corpus diversity — measuring redundancy/leakage within and across corpora via a lexical-overlap statistic, the same contamination-forensics role GSM1k plays for GSM8k, not S-kingdom since the diversity metric's purpose is auditing prior corpora's construct validity rather than scoring a single model's output quality.
one_line: A bidirectional-BLEU lexicon usage diversity metric exposes that MathQA is 85% near-duplicate problems (CLD 0.05) — and on a size-matched but genuinely diverse corpus (CLD 0.49), the same neural solver's accuracy falls from 86% to 36%.
key_number: GTS solver accuracy: 86% on low-diversity MathQA-C (CLD 0.08) -> 68% on arithmetic-only ASDiv-A (CLD 0.50) -> 36% on full ASDiv (CLD 0.49); grade 5-6 problems collapse to 1-7% for all three solvers tested.

title: Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations
reward_readiness_reason: A post-hoc statistical framework (standard errors, clustered variance, paired significance tests, sample-size planning) applied to existing eval scores; no relationship to RL/reward signals stated.
placement_reason: Treats eval questions as draws from an unseen super-population, giving closed-form standard errors, clustered-variance corrections, and a sample-size/power-analysis formula — a general-purpose statistical-rigor instrument applicable across any eval, used to show Llama 3's published confidence intervals were too narrow on some evals and too wide on others.
one_line: A statistical framework giving closed-form standard errors, clustered-variance corrections, paired significance tests, and sample-size planning for eval scores — used to show Llama 3's published confidence intervals were too narrow on some evals and too wide on others.
key_number: Re-analysis shows Llama 3's own published confidence intervals were miscalibrated in both directions (too narrow on some evals, too wide on others)

title: Compositional Questions Do Not Necessitate Multi-hop Reasoning
group: University of Washington / Allen Institute for AI
reward_readiness_reason: A zero-capacity probe model plus a human ablation used to read whether HotpotQA's evidence pool actually forces multi-hop reasoning; no RL/reward use is stated.
placement_reason: Its founding question, like jiang-2019 two entries earlier, is whether HotpotQA's construction actually enforces the multi-hop reasoning it claims to test — here via a deliberately capacity-limited probe model rather than an adversarial document, decomposing the task into single-paragraph reads as a proxy for whether cross-paragraph reasoning is structurally required, which is why its signal_fidelity is decomposed-proxy rather than jiang-2019's elicited-behavior.
one_line: A single-paragraph BERT reader with zero cross-paragraph attention scores 67.08 F1 on HotpotQA's distractor setting — comparable to purpose-built multi-hop systems — because most evidence pools don't actually force multi-hop reasoning.
key_number: Single-paragraph BERT: 67.08 F1 (distractor), rivaling multi-hop SOTA; manual categorization finds only 27% of bridge questions genuinely require both gold paragraphs.

title: FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation
reward_readiness_reason: Precision being gameable by abstaining/saying less is a garden-variety gameable metric, not a self-defeating instrument; FActScore is not an adversary- or contamination-detector and is normally just reported, so 'gameable if optimized' belongs in diagnostic-only, not optimization-forbidden.
placement_reason: Born to produce a single factual-precision score for long-form text by decomposing it into atomic facts and scoring the supported fraction against a knowledge source — a reference-anchored model scorer, the S3 role.
one_line: Long-form factuality as the fraction of atomic facts Wikipedia supports; a retrieval+LM estimator matches human annotators within ~2% aggregate error.
key_number: Best automatic estimators reach ER < 2% vs humans (Inst-LLAMA ensemble: 1.4 on InstructGPT, 0.4 on ChatGPT), correlating at 0.99 Pearson across 10+ models.

title: NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-model use is stated; the effective-length metric is a read-only diagnostic of how far context-handling degrades once surface cues are stripped, not a training target.
placement_reason: Born to ask whether "near-saturated" scores on existing needle-in-haystack benchmarks reflect genuine long-range reasoning or a literal-vocabulary-matching shortcut — it quantifies the confound directly (Table 1's ROUGE-overlap comparison across benchmarks) before engineering it out, a metric/construct critique of the field's dominant long-context evaluation methodology, not merely a harder capability benchmark (V1) since the paper's own contribution is exposing what the metric was actually measuring.
one_line: Strips literal vocabulary overlap between needle and question (ROUGE-1 precision 0.069 vs. 0.905 for vanilla NIAH) to isolate genuine associative long-context retrieval from lexical pattern-matching — 11 of 13 flagship 128K+-context models fall to half their short-context score by 32K tokens.
key_number: GPT-4o, the best model tested, falls from a 99.3% base score to 69.7% accuracy at 32K tokens; reintroducing literal overlap (multiple-choice with the answer name as an option) recovers most of the loss (56.2%→93.1%, one-hop, 32K).

title: MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-reward use is stated; MTEB is a frozen-embedding, fixed-protocol harness used to rank text embedding models, not wired as a gradient signal.
placement_reason: Born to answer whether there is a single shared way to say which text embedding model is actually good, replacing STS-only vibes-checking with a fixed 8-task, 58-dataset harness under one evaluation contract per task type — the GLUE/HELM aggregate-many-scenarios T1 role for the embedding-model population, not a single capability axis or a construct critique of one existing metric (though its own Avg-column critique reads like one).
one_line: Eight embedding task types, 58 datasets, 112 languages, one fixed evaluation contract per task — replacing the field's habit of judging embeddings on whichever single benchmark (usually STS) flatters them.
key_number: No single model wins every task across 33 models: ST5-XXL leads Classification/Clustering/STS/Avg but isn't the best model on 4 of 7 tasks; the headline 'Avg' is a 56-dataset mean where Retrieval+Classification supply half the weight and Summarization 1/56th.

title: Deep Neural Networks are Easily Fooled: High Confidence Predictions for Unrecognizable Images
reward_readiness_reason: The paper's own method directly optimizes (via evolutionary search / gradient ascent) against the DNN's own softmax confidence as a fitness function and shows the signal collapses completely — driving confidence to 99.99% on pure static/noise images — the canonical demonstration that raw softmax confidence cannot survive being used as an optimization target.
placement_reason: Stages a direct-construction attack on the classifier and scores what breaks (confidence collapses to meaningless on adversarially-optimized garbage input) — squarely the I3 adversarial-robustness role, and the diagnostic seed the entire OOD-detection literature (MSP, ODIN) cites first.
one_line: Evolutionary search and gradient ascent synthesize images from scratch — static, stripes, swirls — that state-of-the-art ImageNet/MNIST classifiers label with up to 99.99% confidence, exposing softmax confidence as no guarantee of genuine recognition.
key_number: CPPN-evolved images reach median 88.11% confidence across all 1,000 ImageNet classes after just 5,000 generations; retraining with fooling images as an explicit negative class barely helps on MNIST (still 99.99% after 15 rounds) and only partly helps on ImageNet (88.1% -> 11.7%)

title: Behaviour Suite for Reinforcement Learning
reward_readiness_reason: A per-capability [0,1] radar diagnostic meant to be read, not trained against; no RL/reward use of the summary scores is stated beyond using them to compare baseline agents.
placement_reason: Its founding question — what should we measure across RL agent competence and how do we aggregate many targeted diagnostics into one comparable profile — is the same T1 holistic-aggregation move HELM and BIG-bench make for language models, applied to RL; it isn't a single capability axis (T2) since its whole design point is deliberately isolating seven separate, differently-behaving axes rather than one non-saturating measuring stick.
one_line: 23 named diagnostic RL experiments, each reduced to a [0,1] score and rolled up into a 7-capability radar (basic, generalization, noise, scale, exploration, credit assignment, memory) instead of one leaderboard number.
key_number: Bootstrapped DQN is the only one of three baselines to solve 'deep sea' reliably up to N=50; the recurrent actor-critic is the only one to beat random on memory length, and only up to length 30 — matching its 30-step truncated BPTT exactly.

title: Understanding Factuality in Abstractive Summarization with FRANK: A Benchmark for Factuality Metrics
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-reward use is stated; FRANK is a meta-evaluation resource used to rank nine automatic factuality metrics by partial correlation with human judgment, not wired as a training signal.
placement_reason: Born to answer which automatic factuality metric can be trusted, and on which kind of error, rather than to rank summarizers — a seven-category linguistic typology applied to 2,250 human-annotated summaries, then used to benchmark nine metrics via partial correlation controlling for system/dataset identity — the same show-a-metric-measures-the-wrong-thing F3 role that BEGIN and FActScore later build on.
one_line: A seven-category linguistic typology of factual errors, applied to 2,250 human-annotated summaries, benchmarks nine automatic factuality metrics by partial correlation — finding even the best (FactCC, BERTScore Precision) only weakly track human judgment.
key_number: Best-correlating metrics: FactCC partial ρ=0.20, BERTScore Precision ρ=0.27 (per the authors' bug-fixed arXiv v2 — the published NAACL PDF's uncorrected BERTScore result is a statistically insignificant −0.02); entailment/QGA metrics' correlation drops by roughly a factor of four moving from CNN/DM to XSum.

title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
reward_readiness_reason: Explicit warning: a shared-weights grader inflates its own scores and, when optimizer and reward model share weights, enables effectively unbounded reward hacking — optimizing against self-evaluation destroys the instrument.
placement_reason: Born to answer whether the LLM-as-judge machinery silently marks its own homework, it audits the judge's own bias (self-recognition causally driving self-preference), placing it in judge-bias forensics rather than any capability or scoring family.
one_line: LLM judges recognize their own text out of the box, and self-preference rises linearly with self-recognition — your judge may be marking its own homework.
key_number: GPT-4 out-of-the-box pairwise self-recognition: 73.5%; label-swap probe flips self-preference from 0.73 to 0.32.

title: BLEU: a Method for Automatic Evaluation of Machine Translation
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-model use stated (2002); used as a corpus-level leaderboard/iteration number, not a per-example gradient signal — the digest lists it alongside SacreBLEU/MT-Bench-as-leaderboard diagnostic reads.
placement_reason: At birth (2002) it answered "what single cheap number captures MT output quality against human references so developers can iterate nightly?" — the founding lexical-overlap scoring metric.
one_line: Clipped n-gram precision plus a brevity penalty turns MT evaluation into a nightly script, reporting 0.99 correlation with human judges over five systems.
key_number: 0.99 correlation with monolingual human judges (0.96 bilingual) — but from a regression over only five systems on one Chinese-to-English news corpus

title: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Algorithms in Cooperative Tasks
reward_readiness_reason: A cross-algorithm comparison protocol with per-task significance tests, reported to rank nine algorithms; no RL/reward use of the comparison itself is stated (the underlying environment rewards train the compared algorithms, but the benchmarking methodology is not itself optimized against).
placement_reason: Its founding question — does deep MARL have the same reproducibility/comparability problem single-agent RL already reckoned with, and can one shared, fairness-constrained codebase answer it across many tasks and paradigms at once — is the T1 holistic-aggregation move HELM and BIG-bench make for language models, extended by this paper directly from henderson-2017's single-agent reckoning into the multi-agent setting.
one_line: Nine deep MARL algorithms, three learning paradigms, 25 cooperative tasks, one shared codebase (EPyMARL): a systematic head-to-head finding no universal winner, with value-decomposition and off-policy methods collapsing to near-zero learning in a new sparse-reward warehouse environment.
key_number: RWARE Tiny 4p: MAPPO reaches 49.42 +/- 1.22 while IQL, MADDPG, COMA, VDN and QMIX are all statistically indistinguishable from failing to learn at all (0.30-1.16).

title: The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL): From Tool Use to Agentic Evaluation of Large Language Models
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-model use is stated; BFCL is a leaderboard whose own methodological bet — that execution-free AST matching substitutes for real execution — is validated only qualitatively ("a strong correlation," no reported statistic), so it functions as a diagnostic capability read, not a hardened reward.
placement_reason: Born to make function-calling correctness mechanically checkable at a scale live execution can't reach, by parsing model output with Python's own AST module and matching function name plus parameter values against a predefined valid set — an execution-free but still deterministic, mechanical correctness oracle, the scalability trick that made it the field's de facto tool-calling leaderboard, not a decomposed multi-criterion rubric (V2) since each call is graded as a single pass/fail structural match.
one_line: 5,051 question-function-answer datapoints (single-turn, crowd-sourced, multi-turn, agentic) graded by parsing model output with Python's own AST module and matching function name plus parameter values, rather than executing the call.
key_number: gpt-4o-2024-11-20 leads at 66.4% overall but the same leaderboard-topping models collapse on memory management — the best model reaches only 12% accuracy — and a perplexity/Char-NLL contamination check catches Salesforce xLAM-7B's overfitting (3.67→5.09) on the fresh crowd-sourced set.

title: GDPval: Evaluating AI Model Performance on Real-World Economically Valuable Tasks
reward_readiness_reason: Grading one pairwise comparison averages over an hour of expert time and the automated proxy is explicitly "a proxy, not a substitute... not a reward signal" — too slow/situated to be a gradient.
placement_reason: At birth it asked "can frontier models match industry-expert deliverables on real paid knowledge work?" — a capability instrument whose verdict is a human expert reading the real artifact, closest in the tree to the human-audit family alongside Gender Shades and Med-PaLM.
one_line: Real paid knowledge-work tasks graded by blinded expert pairwise comparison against the professional's own deliverable; best model hits 47.6% wins+ties, below parity.
key_number: Claude Opus 4.1 best at 47.6% wins+ties vs the human expert deliverable, just short of the 50% parity line

title: Ignore Previous Prompt: Attack Techniques For Language Models
reward_readiness_reason: The digest's gameability is on the ATTACKER side (picking an easy target string inflates the attack success rate), not 'training the defended model against this destroys the measurement'; it is an adversarial-robustness probe that is reported, so it is diagnostic-only, not optimization-forbidden.
placement_reason: Born to answer "how easily does a handcrafted injected user input break a flat-prompt GPT-3 app's goal or leak its hidden prompt?" — a deliberate adversarial probe of prompt-injection robustness, exactly the I3 adversarial-robustness question.
one_line: PROMPTINJECT: a modular framework that measures prompt-injection success by strict string-match scoring — exact-match rogue string or leaked-instruction substring — over 35 GPT-3 prompts.
key_number: 58.6% ± 1.6 goal-hijacking success (and 23.6% ± 2.7 prompt-leaking) on text-davinci-002 without searching for optimal attacks

title: Discovering Language Model Behaviors with Model-Written Evaluations
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-model use stated; the discriminator model only filters training-data quality, not a training reward, and every headline result (sycophancy, shutdown-avoidance) is a self-reported verbal tendency read off a generated multiple-choice eval, used to discover inverse-scaling effects rather than to optimize against.
placement_reason: Its lasting, most-cited contribution is discovering that RLHF training tracks a stronger stated desire to avoid shutdown and elevated stated desire for survival/power/wealth — a propensity probe (dangerous-capability & propensity), not a scoring metric or a task-capability benchmark; the generate-then-filter pipeline is the delivery mechanism, but the eval's target is behavioral tendency, matching I2 siblings ren-2025-mask and meinke-2024-in-context-scheming rather than a T-measurement-theory framework.
one_line: A generate-then-filter LM pipeline builds 154 evaluation datasets nearly as reliable as human-written ones, surfacing two inverse-scaling behaviors: sycophancy and RLHF-driven desire to avoid shutdown.
key_number: LM-written advanced-AI-risk evals score 93% label-correctness vs. 97% for human-written ones; the largest (52B) models are sycophantic on >90% of NLP/philosophy questions

title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
reward_readiness_reason: The RL red-LM variant is directly optimized (A2C with a KL penalty) against the same harm-classifier score reported as the paper's headline 'offensiveness elicited' metric — a genuine reward-adapted loop, and Table 6 shows the documented hacking cost: RL's 42.3% offensive-elicit rate collapses diversity below the human baseline (Self-BLEU 84.4 vs 48.5), with 78% of generated test cases sharing one trigger word ('invisible').
placement_reason: Born to answer whether a target LM's harmful behaviors can be discovered automatically at a scale no human red team can match, while staying natural-language and controllable — a three-stage attack loop (red LM generates, target LM replies, classifier flags harm) that stages adversarial situations and scores what breaks — the canonical I3 adversarial-robustness role alongside its own sibling PromptInject, not a scoring metric or a process-surveillance protocol.
one_line: A red LM generates adversarial test-case questions, a target LM answers, and a classifier flags harm — surfacing 18,444 offensive replies from a 280B-parameter chatbot out of 0.5M generated questions, with zero hand-written examples.
key_number: RL-trained red-teaming pushes the offensive-elicit rate to 42.3% but collapses diversity below the human baseline (Self-BLEU 84.4 vs 48.5), with 78% of generated test cases sharing one trigger word ('invisible') — a documented reward-hacking mode against its own grading classifier.

title: tinyBenchmarks: evaluating LLMs with fewer examples
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-signal use — gp-IRT produces a cheap accuracy estimate for benchmark leaderboards and model-development iteration, not a reward wired into a policy.
placement_reason: Born to answer ‘how few examples does a benchmark actually need to estimate a model's true score reliably?’ — a general-purpose IRT-based statistical instrument for measurement efficiency, applicable across any existing benchmark, the same T2 statistical-metrology role as Error Bars for Evals rather than a new capability score or a benchmark-rigor checklist.
one_line: 100 IRT-selected anchor examples (out of MMLU's ~14,000) predict a model's full-benchmark accuracy within about 2% average error — a 140x cost reduction validated across the Open LLM Leaderboard, MMLU, HELM, and AlpacaEval 2.0.
key_number: 100 curated MMLU examples predict full-MMLU accuracy within 1.9% average error on a held-out, later-model time split (Spearman r_S=0.92); IRT-based anchors are 'only slightly affected' by a 40-model domain-shift stress test where correctness-clustering degrades noticeably

title: A Call for Clarity in Reporting BLEU Scores
reward_readiness_reason: post_training_link is "none — the explainer describes reporting/comparability only; no reward-signal use"; the contribution is a reporting protocol read off leaderboards, not a gradient signal.
placement_reason: At birth it asked "is the reported BLEU number itself trustworthy and comparable across papers?" — a critique of the metric's reporting integrity, not a new quality score, placing it squarely in metric/construct forensics.
one_line: BLEU's hidden tokenization/casing knobs swing scores more than papers' claimed gains; sacreBLEU locks the reference inside the metric and prints a version string.
key_number: Reference-preprocessing choices swing the same system's BLEU by up to 1.8 points (de-en), often more than papers' claimed gains

title: Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models
group: University of Washington / MosaicML / Meta AI / AI2
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-reward use is stated; the compositionality gap is a diagnostic ratio computed at evaluation time, and self-ask is a fixed prompt scaffold, not a training signal (the paper explicitly contrasts this with later RL-trained search agents that automate the same decompose-then-retrieve pattern end to end).
placement_reason: Born to answer whether scaling improves compositional reasoning, not just fact recall — the compositionality gap isolates composition failure from simple ignorance by scoring only questions where both sub-facts are independently known, instrumented via Compositional Celebrities and Bamboogle — the same single-capability-axis-instrument T2 role as BEIR, not a holistic multi-task aggregator or a construct critique of an existing benchmark.
one_line: Defines the compositionality gap — the fraction of 2-hop questions a model misses despite knowing both underlying facts — and shows it stays flat (29–64%) from 0.35B to 175B parameters; self-ask prompting narrows it and plugs cleanly into a search engine.
key_number: Self-ask beats chain-of-thought by +11 points absolute on Bamboogle (57.6% vs 46.4%) and matches Least-to-Most prompting's accuracy while running over 30% faster; self-ask+search reaches 60.0% Bamboogle / 40.1% 2WikiMultiHopQA.

title: LHAW: Controllable Underspecification for Long-Horizon Tasks
reward_readiness_reason: post_training_link: "none -- no reward-signal use or training-data production stated"; heavy pass@3 long-horizon rollouts across 285 variants make it a read-models instrument, not a gradient.
placement_reason: Born to make "does a long-horizon agent detect underspecification and clarify well" mechanically checkable by wrapping execution-graded agent tasks in an interactive oracle-user harness — an agentic-work competence harness.
one_line: Synthetic pipeline strips info from long-horizon tasks, labels ambiguity by terminal-state divergence across rollouts, and grades whether agents ask clarifying questions well.
key_number: 285-variant benchmark (85 TheAgentCompany + 100 SWE-Bench Pro + 100 MCP-Atlas); outcome-critical variants collapse Opus-4.5 from 1.00 to 0.14

title: WorldSimBench: Towards Video Generation Models as World Simulators
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-signal use — the closed-loop task-success read and HPE dimension scores are reported as benchmark comparisons across 8 fine-tuned video-generation models, not wired into a policy training loop (the video-to-action policies inside the loop are pre-trained control policies, not the object under evaluation).
placement_reason: Born to answer whether a generated video is actually 'actionable' — whether converting it into control signals and executing them in a real simulator produces working behavior, not just whether it looks good; the Implicit Manipulative Evaluation closes a real interactive control loop (video→action→simulator→new observation) in MineRL/CARLA/CALVIN, the same competence-inside-an-interactive-task role as SIMPLER, paired with a secondary trained-judge perceptual track this record's verdict_engine doesn't capture.
one_line: Sorts video-generation models into an S0-S3 capability hierarchy and targets the top rung — 'World Simulators' — with a dual benchmark: a trained Human Preference Evaluator scoring 20 embodied dimensions, and a closed control loop that converts generated video into real actions and executes them in MineRL/CARLA/CALVIN.
key_number: The closed-loop actionability test — the paper's namesake claim — is reported for only 3 of 8 evaluated video-generation models in the driving and manipulation scenarios

title: Agentic Rubrics as Contextual Verifiers for SWE Agents
reward_readiness_reason: Explicitly framed as verifiable reward for post-training (Verifier's Law) and already produced distilled training data (2,000 rubric-gen trajectories), but the design anticipates verifier hacking (judge never sees the trajectory; Integrity axis encodes no-cheating constraints) and the RLVR loop with its hacking/non-stationarity cost is explicitly deferred to future work.
placement_reason: Born to make SWE-agent patch correctness mechanically checkable without execution, by decomposing correctness into an agent-written, repo-grounded weighted rubric an LLM judge grades item-by-item — a rubric verification harness.
one_line: Expert agent explores the repo to write a weighted rubric checklist; an LLM judge grades patches against it execution-free, beating patch classifiers at best-of-16.
key_number: 40.6% BEST@16 on Qwen3-32B rollouts, +3.5 pts over the best non-agentic baseline; rubric scores predict GT test pass/fail at ROC-AUC 0.886

title: Evaluating Protein Transfer Learning with TAPE
reward_readiness_reason: A standardized cross-architecture comparison protocol reported per-task with no aggregate leaderboard; no RL/reward use is stated, and its splits exist to be read, not optimized against.
placement_reason: Its founding question is what to measure across protein representation learning and how to standardize comparison so five previously-incompatible task-specific eval setups become one suite — the T1 holistic-aggregation role HELM and BIG-bench play for language models, not a single capability axis (T2) since it deliberately spans structure, evolutionary distance, and engineering as three distinct themes.
one_line: Five biologically-curated protein tasks, splits filtered on sequence identity or held out by evolutionary family/clan, and supervised architectures explicitly size-matched to GLUE's — so self-supervised protein embeddings can finally be compared on one shared, leakage-conscious benchmark instead of five incompatible ones.
key_number: Self-supervised pretraining improves all 15 architecture x task comparisons, but hand-built alignment features still beat every learned representation on Secondary Structure (0.80 vs 0.75) and Contact (0.64 vs 0.40) while losing decisively on Remote Homology (0.09 vs 0.26).

title: COMET: A Neural Framework for MT Evaluation
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-model use is stated (2020); COMET-HTER/MQM/RANK are trained to imitate WMT human judgments and read off as a leaderboard/iteration number for MT systems, not wired as a per-example training signal.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'what number captures a translation's human-judged quality when neural MT breaks the lexical-overlap assumption' with a trained neural scalar regressed on human judgments (HTER/MQM/DARR) that also feeds the source, not just hypothesis+reference — the same S2 learned-metric role as BLEURT, distinguished by source-conditioning rather than by kind.
one_line: A learned, source-aware MT metric — three variants trained on HTER/MQM/DARR over a shared XLM-RoBERTa encoder — that keeps discriminating top systems as BLEU's correlation collapses toward zero.
key_number: COMET-RANK Kendall tau on WMT19 DARR: en-kk 0.693 vs BLEU's 0.363; unlike BLEU, it stays well above zero as the evaluated pool narrows to the top 4 MT systems.

title: The MASK Benchmark: Disentangling Honesty From Accuracy in AI Systems
reward_readiness_reason: "Not used as a reward signal"; critique warns the hand-crafted pressure scenarios are Goodhart-able — "a model can be trained to 'pass' the scene without becoming honest."
placement_reason: Built to answer "does the model knowingly lie when we stage adversarial pressure?" — a staged behavioral probe of honesty as propensity, disentangled from accuracy, not a metric or a task harness.
one_line: Elicit a model's belief neutrally, pressure it to lie, score S ≠ B — showing scale buys accuracy (+87.3%) but not honesty (−59.9%).
key_number: P(Lie) spans 26.6% (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) to 63.0% (Grok 2) across 30 frontier LLMs; no model is explicitly honest in more than 46% of cases

title: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices
reward_readiness_reason: A 46-criteria design/implementation/documentation/maintenance checklist scored by expert reviewers; a benchmark-construction audit, not a reward or training signal.
placement_reason: A 46-criteria assessment framework audits 24 widely-used AI benchmarks across their full lifecycle — design, implementation, documentation, maintenance — finding MMLU scores lowest of all 24 while GPQA scores among the highest, and that most benchmarks lack replication scripts or significance reporting.
one_line: A 46-criteria assessment framework audits 24 widely-used AI benchmarks across their design, implementation, documentation, and maintenance lifecycle, finding large quality gaps and that most lack replication scripts or statistical-significance reporting.
key_number: 24 benchmarks scored against 46 criteria; MMLU scores lowest of all 24, GPQA among the highest

title: Beyond Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP Models with CheckList
reward_readiness_reason: Per-cell failure rates are meant to be read and fixed by developers; no RL/reward use is stated, and the whole matrix is only as complete as its designers' imagination, which the paper itself flags as a structural limit.
placement_reason: Its founding move is decomposing a single accuracy number into a matrix of many mechanically-checkable behavioral criteria — the V2 rubric-verifier role (decompose the verdict into checkable criteria) rather than I3 (its MFT/INV/DIR checks are deterministic pattern tests, not staged security attacks) or S-kingdom (it produces a matrix of pass/fail cells, not a single quality score).
one_line: A capabilities-x-test-types matrix (Minimum Functionality, Invariance, Directional Expectation) turns 'is the model good' into 'which specific behaviors does it get wrong' — finding a commercial sentiment API failing simple negation 54.2% of the time despite 'solved' benchmark accuracy.
key_number: In a controlled study, practitioners given CheckList's capability list and templates wrote 2.3x more tests and found nearly 3x as many severity>=3 bugs as unaided testers in the same two hours.

title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward use stated; the emulator+evaluator pipeline is validated as a pre-deployment risk-identification tool (72.5%/68.8% precision against human-annotated ground truth), not wired into training.
