placement_reason: Built to answer whether LM agents will take a dangerous real-world action (wrong payee, destructive command, leaked privacy) when handed ambiguous, underspecified tool-use instructions — an agent-risk propensity probe that emulates the entire sandbox (tools, environment state, evaluator) via LM prompting rather than requiring real API/tool implementations, closest to I2's 'would it, and can the risk be surfaced cheaply' question.
one_line: Prompts GPT-4 to emulate 311 tools across 36 high-stakes toolkits (no real sandboxes built) plus a second LM to judge agent safety, validated against human annotators (72.5%/68.8% precision, 6-of-7 real-sandbox reproductions on Terminal) — even the best 2023 agent configuration still failed 23.9% of 144 underspecified-instruction test cases.
key_number: 6 of 7 ToolEmu-flagged ChatGPT-3.5 Terminal failures reproduced on a real bash sandbox, at under 15 minutes versus the 8 hours it took to build that sandbox by hand

title: ARB: Advanced Reasoning Benchmark for Large Language Models
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward use stated; the rubric-grading pipeline is validated only as GPT-4-grading-GPT-4's-own-solutions on GPT-4-generated rubrics — an unvalidated-beyond-self-agreement diagnostic tool, not demonstrated as a training signal.
placement_reason: ARB's genuinely novel contribution beyond a difficulty-focused benchmark is its GPT-4 rubric-based grading pipeline for open-ended math/physics proofs — decomposing a reference solution into a weighted 10-point rubric and grading a candidate step-by-step against it, the same decompose-the-verdict-into-checkable-criteria move as PaperBench and Agent-as-a-Judge, validated (if narrowly, as grader-self-agreement) against independent human scores at Pearson r=0.78-0.91.
one_line: Sources graduate-level math/physics/law/MCAT problems from low-web-visibility problem books and exam material, mixing multiple-choice with numerical/symbolic/open-ended-proof formats to resist saturation; a GPT-4 rubric grader for open-ended answers correlates with human scores at Pearson r=0.78-0.91, though validated only as GPT-4-grading-itself on GPT-4-written rubrics.
key_number: GPT-4 leads every category yet stays under 20% on Physics Numerical and under 5% on Math Numerical, even while topping 80-87% on the MCAT multiple-choice splits

title: Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?
reward_readiness_reason: post_training_link: "none — the paper feeds no reward signal; its stated payoff is methodological hygiene for benchmark builders" — it is a metric-ablation read of curves, not a gradient signal.
placement_reason: At birth it asked "is the 'emergent ability' verdict a property of the model or an artifact of the scoring metric?" — a critique of the measurement instrument itself (metric choice deforming smooth loss into a false cliff), which is exactly the F3 metric-and-construct-critique role.
one_line: Emergent-ability cliffs are artifacts of harsh nonlinear metrics: re-score identical outputs with linear or continuous metrics and they flatten into smooth ramps.
key_number: >92% of all claimed emergent abilities on BIG-Bench appear under only two metrics: Multiple Choice Grade (76.1%) and Exact String Match (16.4%)

title: QuestEval: Summarization Asks for Fact-based Evaluation
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-reward use is stated; QuestEval is a post-hoc scoring pipeline (QG+QA models plus a learned weighter) used to rank summaries by correlation with human judgment, not wired as a gradient signal.
placement_reason: Born to unify prior QA-based metrics' split precision (Wang et al./QAGS) and recall (Scialom et al./SummaQA) signals into one reference-free score against the source document, the first QA-based metric reported to beat ROUGE/BERTScore on human correlation — the canonical S3 reference-free-scorer role.
one_line: Unifies a QA-based precision score (questions from the summary, checked against the source) and a learned-weight recall score (questions from the source, checked against the summary) into one reference-free harmonic mean.
key_number: Reaches 33.5 average Pearson correlation on SummEval with zero references vs BERTScore-f's 23.1 with 11 references — though the paper's own ablation grid shows the simpler Precision-Only variant, not the recommended learned-weighter config, tops three of the five result grids it reports (Consistency 46.5, Fluency 30.9, all of QAGS-XSUM 32.7).

title: PropensityBench: Evaluating Latent Safety Risks in Large Language Models via an Agentic Approach
reward_readiness_reason: Benignly renaming the forbidden tool nearly 4x's o4-mini's propensity (15.8%->59.3%), so the metric keys on surface cues — training against it teaches pattern-matching, not alignment, destroying the instrument.
placement_reason: Built to answer whether a model will knowingly misuse a dangerous capability when the safe path is blocked and pressure escalates — a staged behavioral propensity probe, not a capability or metric audit.
one_line: Agentic trap benchmark: rig the safe tool to always fail, escalate pressure, and mechanically count how often models knowingly invoke a forbidden proxy tool.
key_number: Average propensity to invoke the forbidden tool hits 46.9% at maximum pressure vs near-zero at rest.

title: BLEURT: Learning Robust Metrics for Text Generation
reward_readiness_reason: "No post_training_link in the paper itself — it predates reward-hacking work"; a learned black-box scalar used to rank MT/data-to-text outputs by human-correlation, not wired as a gradient signal.
placement_reason: Born to answer "what number captures a generated text's human-judged quality?" with a trained neural scalar that beats surface n-gram overlap — the canonical learned metric.
one_line: Mid-train BERT on ~6.5M synthetic perturbations before rating fine-tuning: a learned text-quality metric that survives quality drift where IID-trained metrics collapse.
key_number: WMT17 avg over 7 to-English pairs: BLEURT Kendall tau 62.5 / Pearson r 81.8 vs BERTScore-RoBERTa 58.0 / 76.8 and sentence-BLEU 32.4 / 47.5

title: PrivacyLens: Evaluating Privacy Norm Awareness of Language Models in Action
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-signal use — leakage rate is reported as a benchmark comparison metric across nine models and two prompt conditions, not wired into a policy training loop.
placement_reason: Born to make 'did the agent leak private information' mechanically checkable inside a real tool-use trajectory, rather than relying on probing questions the paper shows diverge sharply from actual behavior — an interactive-task harness (seed → vignette → executable ToolEmu trajectory → automated leak/helpfulness classification) in the same V3 competence-inside-a-task role as MathDial/MRBench/LHAW, not a staged single-shot behavioral probe.
one_line: 493 Contextual-Integrity seeds become vignettes and executable ToolEmu agent trajectories, probed with QA questions at three levels and checked for real leakage in the agent's final tool-use action — GPT-4 answers 98.99% of probing questions correctly yet still leaks in 25.68% of its actual actions.
key_number: GPT-4 adjusted leakage rate 25.68% (Privacy-Enhancing Prompt) despite 98.99% trajectory-level probing accuracy; Llama-3-70B-Instruct leaks in 38.69% of actions under the same conditions

title: The Leaderboard Illusion
reward_readiness_reason: An observational audit of Chatbot Arena's own operational data (testing volume, data access, deprecation); not a reward or training signal.
placement_reason: An audit of 2M Chatbot Arena battles across 243 models and 42 providers finding undisclosed private testing, asymmetric data access, and silent model deprecation that systematically favor a handful of proprietary providers — a rigor audit of the field's most-cited human-preference leaderboard.
one_line: An audit of 2M Chatbot Arena battles across 243 models and 42 providers finds undisclosed private testing (Meta tested 27 variants before Llama 4), asymmetric data access, and silent deprecation of 205 of 243 models.
key_number: Google and OpenAI received an estimated 19.2% and 20.4% of all Arena battle data respectively; 205 of 243 models silently deprecated

title: Large Language Models Encode Clinical Knowledge
reward_readiness_reason: post_training_link: "none as an RL/RLHF reward — the clinician-rated axes are a diagnostic verdict, not a training signal"; alignment came from instruction prompt tuning on 40 clinician-curated exemplars, not optimizing against the eval.
placement_reason: At birth the paper's problem was that multiple-choice accuracy and BLEU miss clinical safety, so it built a nine-clinician panel to audit long-form medical answers for harm, bias, and consensus alignment — a harm/safety audit instrument, not a training reward.
one_line: Medical LLM judged by a nine-clinician panel rating long-form answers on twelve safety axes, alongside multiple-choice accuracy with self-consistency voting.
key_number: Scientific-consensus alignment on 140 long-form questions: Flan-PaLM 61.9% → Med-PaLM 92.6%, vs clinicians 92.9%

title: MultiChallenge: A Realistic Multi-Turn Conversation Evaluation Benchmark Challenging to Frontier LLMs
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-model use is stated; MultiChallenge functions as a leaderboard/development benchmark, and its own critique flags that the benchmarked models also built and filtered the benchmark — a reason its score should stay a diagnostic ranking rather than a hardened training target.
placement_reason: Built to answer "how do we grade an open-ended, no-gold-answer multi-turn response reliably" by collapsing the hard holistic judgment into one easy, human-authored binary rubric question per example graded on the final response alone — the decomposition trick, not the four failure categories themselves, is the paper's own stated transferable contribution, and it became the template HealthBench and PRBench reused.
one_line: 273 expert-edited multi-turn conversations engineered so at least 3 of 6 frontier models fail each one; a single binary yes/no rubric question per example, scored only on the final response, lifts LLM-judge/human agreement from 37.3% to 93.9%.
key_number: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Jun 2024) leads at 41.42%, o1-preview 37.23%, with every frontier model under 50% and GPT-4o at just 12.52%.

title: A Holistic Approach for Test and Evaluation of Large Language Models
reward_readiness_reason: Digest post_training_link: "None - the entropy gate and layered red team are triage/evaluation machinery; reports no use as an RL/preference reward" — human-gated, situated triage, not a gradient signal.
placement_reason: Born to answer "when can we trust an LLM judge (and a layered red team)?" — its experiments chiefly quantify the GPT-4 grader's self-bias and calibrate an entropy gate, i.e. auditing the measurement itself.
one_line: Entropy-gated GPT-4 judging auto-labels confident pairwise verdicts and routes the rest to humans; layered automated-to-generalist-to-expert red teaming covers safety.
key_number: GPT-4 grader agrees 53.8% when humans preferred GPT-4's response vs 76.1% when they preferred the human rewrite (self-bias, Table 2)

title: A Study of Translation Edit Rate with Targeted Human Annotation
reward_readiness_reason: No RL use (2006); the paper flags that annotators were explicitly 'coached on how to minimize the edit rate' before building the gold targeted references used to validate HTER — a metric-shaping-its-own-ground-truth caveat — but the numbers are reported as a leaderboard/protocol comparison, not a gradient signal.
placement_reason: Built as an alternative, more intuitive lexical-overlap metric (edit distance rather than n-gram matching) directly rivaling BLEU/NIST/METEOR on the same DARPA-era corpora — the same founding S1 family, distinguished by a genuine, principled contrast (one coherent edit script vs. n-gram counting) rather than a construct critique of them.
one_line: Scores MT by minimum edit distance (insertions, deletions, substitutions, block shifts) to a reference; its human-targeted variant HTER correlates with average human judgment (0.630) better than two independent human judges agree with each other (0.478).
key_number: HTER correlates with human judgment at 0.630, exceeding the 0.478 inter-human-judge agreement ceiling — though annotators were explicitly coached on how TER counts edits before building the 'gold' targeted references

title: Beyond the Imitation Game: Quantifying and Extrapolating the Capabilities of Language Models
reward_readiness_reason: The canary GUID + training_on_test_set probe exist precisely to keep BIG-bench out of training data — the paper's explicit stance is anti-training-exposure, so optimizing against it destroys the instrument.
placement_reason: Built to escape the SuperGLUE saturation treadmill by assembling 204 beyond-current-model tasks into a single normalized aggregate and reframing evaluation as forecasting which capabilities emerge at which scale — a holistic measurement framework, not a single scorer or oracle.
one_line: 204 crowd-sourced hard tasks auto-graded onto an author-anchored 0-100 scale, reframing evaluation as forecasting which capabilities switch on with scale.
key_number: 204 tasks assembled by 450 authors across 132 institutions; best 2022 models score <20 on the 0-100 human-normalized aggregate while expert raters approach 100

title: PaperBench: Evaluating AI's Ability to Replicate AI Research
reward_readiness_reason: post_training_link: "None — framed as a capability/autonomy measurement instrument for safety frameworks... not as a training reward"; grading costs ~$66/paper and rollouts ~$400 over 12h — too slow/expensive/situated for a gradient signal.
placement_reason: At birth it answered "how do we make 'replicate this ML paper' mechanically checkable?" by decomposing each paper into thousands of author-co-written binary rubric leaves graded by an LLM judge — a rubric verification harness, not a scoring metric or a preference court.
one_line: Agents replicate ML papers from scratch; an o3-mini judge grades 8,316 author-co-written binary rubric leaves, weighted-averaged into a Replication Score.
key_number: 8,316 binary rubric leaf criteria across 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight/Oral papers; best agent (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) scores 21.0% vs 41.4% human baseline; judge F1 = 0.83

title: JudgeBench: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Judges
reward_readiness_reason: Tests whether an LLM judge's verdict matches an objectively correct label drawn from each source dataset's own verifier; diagnostic of judge quality, not itself a training-time reward signal.
placement_reason: Where MT-Bench and Arena-Hard test whether a judge's verdict matches human style preference, JudgeBench tests whether the judge can tell objectively correct from incorrect at all on deliberately style-matched, hard pairs — most vanilla judges can't beat chance.
one_line: 350 objectively correct-vs-incorrect response pairs across knowledge, reasoning, math, and coding, sampled from a single strong model so pairs are style-matched — vanilla-prompted GPT-4o scores just 50.86% at telling right from wrong.
key_number: Vanilla GPT-4o: 50.86% (near chance); best reasoning-heavy judge o3-mini-high: 80.86%

title: BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models
reward_readiness_reason: "Not a reward signal, but a documented optimization target: later retrievers (Contriever, GTR, E5) were explicitly built and tuned against the BEIR leaderboard" — a leaderboard read, not a gradient signal.
placement_reason: At birth BEIR was built to answer "does in-domain retrieval skill transfer out-of-distribution?" — a single capability axis (zero-shot IR generalization) instrumented by a standardized multi-dataset protocol, which is exactly the T2 capability-axis-instrument role alongside Time-Horizons and Monkeys.
one_line: Zero-shot IR benchmark: nDCG@10 vs pooled judgments over 18 datasets; BM25 is hard to beat — partly a lexical annotation-bias artifact.
key_number: 18 datasets across 9 retrieval tasks; 10 systems across 5 architecture families, all evaluated zero-shot on nDCG@10

title: Judging the Judges: Evaluating Alignment and Vulnerabilities in LLMs-as-Judges
reward_readiness_reason: This is a meta-evaluation/audit of judge machinery (like koo-2023-cobbler and wang-2023-fair-evaluators, both diagnostic-only): it READS judges' leniency and gullibility so you can trust or fix them, and the documented gameability is that JUDGES are gameable, not that this audit self-destructs under optimization.
placement_reason: At birth its question was "is the LLM-as-judge measurement itself lying?" — it audits judge reliability against near-ground-truth human labels on a deliberately unambiguous task, exposing leniency and gullibility that aggregate agreement hides.
one_line: Even on trivially clean factual QA, only frontier-size LLM judges near human agreement — and percent agreement flatters everyone; report Scott's pi.
key_number: Humans agree 98.52% (Scott's pi 96.2), but the best judges (GPT-4 Turbo, Llama-3 70B) reach only pi 88 — ~8 points below the human ceiling

title: Unbiased Look at Dataset Bias
reward_readiness_reason: No RL use (2011); a diagnostic audit of dataset bias whose explicit payoff is measurement hygiene for benchmark builders, not a training signal.
placement_reason: At birth it asked 'is a benchmark accuracy score really measuring general capability, or is it partly measuring which specific dataset a model was trained/tested on' — a construct-validity critique of what benchmark accuracy captures, the same F3 role Schaeffer's later emergent-abilities critique plays for capability metrics.
one_line: A linear classifier names which of twelve popular vision datasets a photo came from at 39% accuracy (chance 8%), and a standard detector trained on one dataset loses up to 73% of its accuracy tested on another — 'benchmark accuracy' is partly a dataset fingerprint, not a stand-in for general visual recognition.
key_number: Cross-dataset car-detection AP falls from 53.4% self-test to 27.5% averaged across five foreign test sets (a 48% relative drop); Caltech-101, the most 'inbred' dataset, drops 73% (96.9% -> 26.7%)

title: Towards Conversational Diagnostic AI
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-signal use for the OSCE evaluation itself — the rubric-based specialist/patient-actor ratings are a diagnostic AMIE-vs-PCP comparison protocol, not wired as a reward; AMIE's own self-play training loop instead uses a separate LLM critic on a handful of communication axes, not the OSCE rubric.
placement_reason: Born to test whether an LLM can run the diagnostic interview itself, not just answer questions about clinical information already collected — a randomized, blinded OSCE against real physicians, scored on real clinical-assessment rubrics (GMCPQ/PACES/PCCBP) by specialist physicians and patient actors, the same broad human-expert-panel capability-audit role as Med-PaLM and GDPval, not a factuality metric or a mechanical task harness.
one_line: AMIE, a PaLM 2 model trained via self-play on simulated diagnostic dialogue, out-diagnosed 20 board-certified PCPs in a blinded, randomized, 149-scenario remote OSCE scored on real clinical-assessment rubrics (GMCPQ/PACES/PCCBP) — but was statistically tied with PCPs on confabulation, escalation, and follow-up.
key_number: AMIE beat PCPs on 28 of 32 specialist-rated and 24 of 26 patient-actor-rated axes, but was not significantly better on 4 safety-relevant axes including Confabulation Absent (all n=149)

title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-signal use or anti-optimization warning stated in the paper itself (published mid-2023, before the CoT-monitorability RL wave) — it establishes the faithfulness-measurement methodology later M-kingdom papers (Baker et al., Korbak et al.) explicitly build the 'don't train against the monitor' warning on top of.
placement_reason: The founding CoT-faithfulness test: engineers a counterfactual (reorder answer choices, suggest an answer) that provably moves the model's prediction, then checks whether the verbalized chain-of-thought ever mentions it — establishing the faithfulness-test paradigm (not a capability benchmark or a scoring metric) that Baker et al.'s and Korbak et al.'s CoT-monitorability line explicitly build on.
one_line: Reorders multiple-choice options or suggests an answer, provably moving GPT-3.5/Claude 1.0's predictions by up to 36.3 points on BIG-Bench Hard — yet the models' chain-of-thought explanations never mention the injected bias, and 73% actively rationalize the bias-consistent wrong answer.
key_number: GPT-3.5 zero-shot CoT accuracy drops 36.3 points (59.6% to 23.3%) under the Suggested Answer bias, with the CoT never verbalizing the bias in 234 hand-reviewed cases

title: VeRO: An Evaluation Harness for Agents to Optimize Agents
reward_readiness_reason: The digest states the gated per-commit eval scores ARE the optimization signal the coding agent searches against, and the anti-Goodhart controls (budget gate, no test peeking) exist so the metric CAN be safely optimized against, not forbidden from it; a metric explicitly wired in as the optimization target with documented gaming vectors it must block is reward-adapted, not optimization-forbidden.
placement_reason: At birth VeRO's problem is making "coding agents optimizing another agent's program" a fair, reproducible comparison by decomposing task competence into budget-gated, access-controlled per-commit reward checks — a rubric-verifier harness (the LOCKED rubric fixes VeRO to V2), not a raw execution oracle or a task dataset.
one_line: Budget-gated, permission-controlled harness making "coding agents optimizing agents" measurable; harness access, not the optimizer model, drives the +8-point lift.
key_number: Full VeRO-Agent Default lifts average score 0.50 -> 0.61 (+8 points) vs +2 for Claude Code with VeRO tools and ~0 for prompt-only (GPT-4.1-mini target, B=8).

title: CIDEr: Consensus-based Image Description Evaluation
reward_readiness_reason: "No use as a training reward is stated in the explainer; the connection is defensive" — the paper builds CIDEr-D to resist gaming rather than to serve as a reward, and it is an aggregate/reference-based scorer used to read caption quality, not train.
placement_reason: At birth CIDEr answered "what number captures a caption's quality?" by defining a TF-IDF n-gram overlap score against human references — the canonical lexical-overlap scoring metric alongside BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR.
one_line: Scores a caption by TF-IDF n-gram cosine against ~50 human references, targeting consensus human-likeness; became the COCO server's default captioning metric.
key_number: At 48 references, CIDEr reaches 84% agreement with human consensus (90% human ceiling), vs BLEU1/ROUGE1 at 76%/74% on PASCAL-50S at the standard 5 references.

title: The AI Productivity Index (APEX)
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-model use is stated; scores are a rubric-pass-rate leaderboard, and the critique's central finding — an unvalidated single-vendor judge grading its own provider's models with no reported human-agreement check — means the signal is not shown safe to optimize against.
placement_reason: Decomposes deliverable "quality" into discrete Pass/Fail criteria the authors themselves call "unit tests for a deliverable," graded by an LM judge — the canonical V2 rubric-verifier design (matching GDPval's real-paid-work framing but replacing GDPval's blinded human pairwise-comparison grading with an automated, decomposed rubric), which is exactly what distinguishes it from GDPval's I4 human-grading placement.
one_line: 137 vetted practitioners across four high-paid knowledge jobs author source-grounded deliverables with roughly 15 Pass/Fail "unit test" criteria each; a single Gemini 2.5 Flash judge grades every model's response, 8 runs per task with 95% CIs.
key_number: GPT-5 (thinking=high) leads at 67.0% of criteria met, with investment banking hardest (63.0%) and law easiest (77.9%); run-to-run SD averages 9.05 points, wider than most adjacent-model gaps, and no LM-vs-human agreement statistic is reported for the single-vendor judge.

title: Building a Question Answering Test Collection
reward_readiness_reason: Pre-RL era (2000); mean reciprocal rank is reported as a shared-task leaderboard number for a NIST track, not a gradient signal, and no optimization-vs-metric relationship is discussed anywhere in the paper.
placement_reason: At birth it asked not just 'what is the leaderboard number' but 'does the document-retrieval evaluation recipe (pooled judgments, a reusable test collection) actually transfer to a task whose unit of judgment is an answer string' — a founding capability-measurement instrument that studies its own protocol's reliability, the same T2 role BEIR later plays for zero-shot IR and Time-Horizons plays for agentic capability.
one_line: Three independent assessors grade every candidate answer string by mean reciprocal rank over a 528K-document collection; system rankings survive assessor disagreement (Kendall's tau .9146-.9976) even though a truly reusable test collection remains unsolved.
key_number: Mean 3-assessor overlap on correct-answer sets .641 (about 6% of judgments contested), yet system-ranking Kendall's tau spans .9146-.9976 across 100,000 resampled single-judge qrels

title: Understanding Contrastive Representation Learning through Alignment and Uniformity on the Hypersphere
reward_readiness_reason: The paper directly trains encoders on L_align + L_uniform alone, with no contrastive loss and no negative sampling at all, and this matches or beats contrastive learning on STL-10, NYU-Depth-V2, and ImageNet(-100) — a clean demonstration the diagnostic survives being optimized against directly, because here it doubles as the training objective.
placement_reason: Its founding move is a computed, reference-free statistic derived from a model's own embedding geometry that stands in for expensive downstream evaluation — the S2 role a fitted/learned score plays (matching lee-2018-mahalanobis's OOD confidence score in mechanism, if not construct), not F3 since it isn't auditing an existing metric's validity but proposing and directly validating a new one via causal ablation.
one_line: Two cheap, differentiable properties of an encoder's output geometry — alignment (do positive pairs land close) and uniformity (do features spread evenly on the hypersphere) — that the contrastive loss provably optimizes asymptotically, and that track downstream accuracy well enough to train on directly.
key_number: Optimizing L_align+L_uniform alone (no contrastive loss) matches or beats the best contrastive-only encoder on STL-10 (81.15% vs 80.46%), NYU-Depth-V2, and ImageNet-100 (74.60% vs 72.80%) — but loses on both BookCorpus sentence tasks, the one non-vision modality tested.

title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
reward_readiness_reason: post_training_link: "Not itself a reward signal" — it audits and calibrates the judge so preference labels are trustworthy before they feed training; it reads/fixes judges rather than serving as a gradient.
placement_reason: At birth it asked "is the LLM judge itself lying?" — diagnosing positional bias in the Vicuna/MT-Bench pairwise judge with a swap-order Conflict Rate and proposing calibration, the defining move of a judge-bias audit.
one_line: LLM judges flip verdicts when answer order swaps; reason-first prompting, both-order averaging, and entropy-gated human review restore human-level agreement.
key_number: With ChatGPT as judge, Vicuna-13B's win rate vs ChatGPT swings from 2.5% (placed first) to 82.5% (placed second) — a 66-of-80 'victory' from seating order alone

title: PandaLM: An Automatic Evaluation Benchmark for LLM Instruction Tuning Optimization
reward_readiness_reason: PandaLM is used in-paper as a selection criterion across 800 pairwise hyperparameter-configuration tournaments to pick better instruction-tuning recipes — an iterative-selection/optimization use beyond pure diagnostic reporting, though a discrete tournament-based selection rather than a differentiable per-example reward.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'can an open, offline, reproducible judge LLM replace API-based GPT-3.5/GPT-4 judging for picking among instruction-tuned checkpoints?' — distilled from GPT-3.5 pairwise comparisons and filtered for position-bias consistency, the defining P2 judge-protocol move, validated by beating Alpaca's default hyperparameter recipe under every judge tested.
one_line: Distills GPT-3.5 pairwise judgments (filtered for position-bias consistency) into an offline LLaMA-based judge; PandaLM-70B edges past GPT-4 on accuracy against 1K human labels (0.6687 vs 0.6647) and its picks beat Alpaca's default hyperparameter recipe under every judge tested.
key_number: PandaLM-selected hyperparameters beat Alpaca-default-tuned models by 79.8 human wins vs 25.2 losses (of 170 test instructions) across five base models

title: Long-form factuality in large language models
reward_readiness_reason: Precision-style gameability (F1@K can be inflated by repeating supported facts up to K) is a garden-variety gameable diagnostic metric, not a self-defeating instrument; SAFE is normally just reported as a leaderboard score, not wired into an RL loop.
placement_reason: Born to extend fact-level decomposed scoring (FActScore's single-domain biography setting) to broad-topic, long-form factuality — SAFE decomposes a response into atomic facts and verifies each against live search, the same S3 decomposed-scorer role FActScore defined, now validated to beat the human annotators it replaces.
one_line: LongFact (2,280 GPT-4-generated fact-seeking prompts across 38 topics) paired with SAFE, a search-augmented LLM agent that decomposes a response into atomic facts and verifies each against Google Search — SAFE agrees with human annotators 72% of the time and wins 76% of adjudicated disagreements, at roughly 1/20th the cost.
key_number: SAFE-human agreement 72.0% on 16,011 facts; SAFE wins 76% of adjudicated disagreements (vs 19% for the original human labels) at $0.19 vs $4.00/response

title: Best Practices for Biorisk Evaluations on Open-Weight Bio-Foundation Models
reward_readiness_reason: Not a reward and not a monitorability-style protected instrument; it is a red-team audit of a training-time mitigation (data filtering), used to read whether excluded capability persists — diagnostic.
placement_reason: Born to test whether pretraining-data filtering actually removes a dangerous capability or merely hides it — a dangerous-capability-recovery probe, asking 'can the excluded skill be fine-tuned or probed back?'
one_line: Red-teams data-filtering as a safety mitigation: excluded capability returns in 0.72 GPU-hours and a zero-update linear probe shows the signal never left the representations.
key_number: Held-out-species perplexity recovers to benign level in 50 fine-tuning steps (0.72 H100 GPU-hours); zero-fine-tune probe hits |rho|=0.159, 52.8% above the no-biology floor.

title: Human Preference Score v2: A Solid Benchmark for Evaluating Human Preferences of Text-to-Image Synthesis
reward_readiness_reason: No in-paper demonstration of using HPS v2 as a training reward or selection signal (unlike ImageReward's ReFL or PickScore's best-of-100 reranking) — the paper's own experiments are entirely diagnostic: benchmarking 20 T2I checkpoints and validating generalization across held-out generator families.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'does a preference-trained scorer generalize across text-to-image generator families it never trained on, not just within one?' — fixing HPS v1/ImageReward/Pick-a-Pic's single-generator and style-word-prompt biases with a 9-generator-plus-COCO test split and ChatGPT-cleaned prompts, the same trained-neural-scorer mechanism as its predecessors, explicitly stress-tested for cross-generator transfer.
one_line: Fixes HPS v1/ImageReward/Pick-a-Pic's single-generator and style-word-prompt biases with a 798,090-comparison dataset spanning nine T2I generators plus real photos and ChatGPT-cleaned prompts; the resulting CLIP-H scorer beats all five prior metrics on both its own test set (83.3%) and ImageReward's external test set (65.7%), though the external-test margin over ImageReward itself is a thin 0.6 points.
key_number: HPS v2 reaches 83.3% agreement on its own 9-generator test set vs PickScore's 79.8%, but only 65.7% vs ImageReward's own 65.1% on ImageReward's external test set

title: Style Over Substance: Evaluation Biases for Large Language Models
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward use stated; it is a diagnostic bias audit of Elo-based LLM-judge evaluation, reading judge behavior under controlled defect injection rather than serving as a training signal.
placement_reason: Born to answer whether Elo-based pairwise LLM-judge evaluation rewards genuine quality or surface properties (length, order, fluency) — isolating the confound by injecting controlled defects into one verified-correct answer rather than comparing different models' natural outputs, exposing GPT-4 rating fabricated facts above a correct-but-short answer; the defining judge-bias-audit move alongside CoBBLEr and FairEval.
one_line: Injects controlled defects (factual errors, length, grammar) into one verified-correct answer to isolate judge bias from genuine quality; GPT-4 rates 'Several Minor Factual Errors' at 1206 Elo above a correct-but-short answer at 1096 Elo, and every judge type favors longer answers 51.9-67.9% of the time.
key_number: Human judges reach only 'slight' Cohen's-kappa agreement with each other and with LLM judges (kappa 0.08-0.14); only GPT-4 and Claude-1 agree at a 'moderate' level (kappa=0.51)

title: ImageReward: Learning and Evaluating Human Preferences for Text-to-Image Generation
reward_readiness_reason: ImageReward's own second contribution, ReFL, back-propagates the reward model's gradient directly into a diffusion model's weights from a randomly sampled late denoising step — a reward model built and used explicitly as a training-time optimization target, the canonical reward-native case.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'what scalar captures human preference over text-to-image generations, trained directly on pairwise human comparisons rather than embedding similarity?' — a BLIP-backed trained neural scorer in BLEURT's learned-metric mold, whose scalar output doubles as ReFL's direct training-time reward gradient.
one_line: A 136,892-comparison expert annotation pipeline trains a BLIP-backed reward scorer that beats CLIP/Aesthetic/BLIP scores by 7-19 points on preference accuracy, and ReFL back-propagates that reward's gradient through a diffusion model's denoising chain — though independent re-evaluations by Pick-a-Pic and HPS v2 find markedly weaker cross-generator generalization.
key_number: ImageReward reaches 65.14% preference accuracy on its own test set, but Pick-a-Pic's independent re-evaluation gets only 61.1%, and on HPS v2's nine-generator test set it falls to second-worst of six models compared (74.0%)

title: SUPERB: Speech processing Universal PERformance Benchmark
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-reward use is stated; SUPERB is a frozen-representation, lightweight-head evaluation protocol used to compare and rank pretrained speech encoders, not a gradient signal.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'how reusable is a frozen SSL speech representation, with minimal downstream adaptation' across four genuinely different facets (content, speaker, semantics, paralinguistics) via ten shared, standardized tasks — the GLUE/HELM playbook of aggregating many scenarios under one fixed protocol, transplanted from text into speech, not a single capability-axis instrument or a metric-validity audit.
one_line: Freezes 14 SSL speech encoders, bolts on the lightest possible task head, and scores them across 10 tasks spanning content/speaker/semantics/paralinguistics — the GLUE playbook transplanted into speech.
key_number: HuBERT Large wins 8 of 12 scored metric columns, but wav2vec 2.0 Large and HuBERT Base split the remaining four (KS/SD and QbE/ASV) — HuBERT Base beats Large on QbE by more than 2x (0.0736 vs 0.0353 MTWV).

title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
reward_readiness_reason: pass^k is a repeated-trials reliability statistic reported on top of an existing task-success oracle; no RL/reward-model use is stated — it's a benchmark score, not a training signal.
placement_reason: Introduces pass^k — the fraction of tasks an agent solves on ALL of k independent trials, a non-saturating reliability axis distinct from Codex's pass@k (at least one of k) — a new capability-axis measuring stick for consistency rather than raw solve rate.
one_line: Introduces pass^k, a reliability statistic measuring whether an agent succeeds on ALL of k repeated trials rather than at least one — gpt-4o's τ-bench pass^8 falls below 25% even though its single-trial success rate is 48.2%.
key_number: gpt-4o pass^1 48.2% vs. pass^8 <25% on τ-bench — reliability collapses far faster than single-trial success would suggest

title: HELMET: How to Evaluate Long-Context Language Models Effectively and Thoroughly
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-signal use — HELMET's seven category scores and correlation analysis are a diagnostic benchmark-selection guide for long-context model development, not wired into a training loop.
placement_reason: Born to answer 'what should we measure to know whether a long-context model actually uses its context window, and how do we aggregate that comparably across models' — seven genuinely distinct application-centric categories standardized to 128K tokens across 59 models, the same taxonomize-and-standardize holistic-framework role as HELM (whose title HELMET's own title echoes), not a single capability-axis instrument or a new scoring metric.
one_line: Needle-in-a-haystack correlates with real long-context downstream performance at only ρ≤0.68 across 35 models, so HELMET evaluates 59 LCLMs across seven application-centric categories at up to 128K tokens with a human-validated model-based metric replacing ROUGE.
key_number: No synthetic recall task exceeds ρ=0.8 correlation with real downstream categories; cross-category correlation ranges from 0.92 (RAG↔LongQA) down to 0.34 (Cite↔ICL) — the seven categories are measuring substantially different capabilities

title: Fairness Beyond Disparate Treatment & Disparate Impact: Learning Classification without Disparate Mistreatment
reward_readiness_reason: No RL use (2016); a supervised fairness-constrained training method reported via disparity metrics (D_FPR/D_FNR), not an RL reward — though the paper's own cited impossibility results mean every one of its 'fair' COMPAS classifiers has, by construction, given up calibration, a cost it never reports.
placement_reason: Names a third fairness construct (disparate mistreatment) that neither disparate treatment nor disparate impact catches, formalized via five candidate rate-equality measures (OMR/FPR/FNR/FDR/FOR) — a construct-naming-and-critique contribution in the same F3 family as its 2016 fairness-impossibility contemporaries, not merely a training method.
one_line: Names disparate mistreatment — unequal misclassification rates across groups, distinct from disparate treatment and disparate impact — and trains against it directly via a covariance proxy that turns a non-convex rate-equality constraint into a convex-concave program; on COMPAS, the Black/white FPR gap falls from 0.35/0.17 to 0.03-0.06 for under one accuracy point.
key_number: On synthetic Case II (D_FPR and D_FNR share a sign), a naive reweighting baseline collapses to 38% accuracy under both constraints, versus 69% for this paper's method and 67% for Hardt et al.

title: AIR-Bench 2024: A Safety Benchmark Based on Risk Categories from Regulations and Policies
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-signal use — refusal rate is reported as a compliance benchmark for comparing models against specific regulations/policies, not wired into a training loop (though the paper's own public-prompt release is a contamination risk it doesn't address, not an in-paper RL use).
placement_reason: Born to answer whether a safety benchmark's risk taxonomy actually maps onto what regulators and companies wrote down, rather than researcher intuition — turning 314 regulation-and-policy-derived risk categories into staged risky prompts and measuring refusal, the same staged-prompt-and-score-what-breaks role as HarmBench, now grounded in an external, auditable taxonomy instead of ad hoc category design.
one_line: 314 risk categories distilled from 8 government regulations and 16 corporate AI policies turned into 5,694 prompts with category-specific GPT-4o autograders (Kappa 0.86 vs humans) — even the best-aligned model family averages only ~71% refusal against the EU AI Act's own risk tiers.
key_number: Prior benchmarks cover only a fraction of AIR 2024's 45 level-3 categories: HEx-PHI 51%, HarmBench 26%, SALAD-Bench 71% — 21 of 45 (46%) are studied by at most one of the three

title: A Careful Examination of Large Language Model Performance on Grade School Arithmetic
reward_readiness_reason: "Not a reward signal itself — it is an anti-Goodhart diagnostic... explicitly warns against optimizing on public benchmarks"; publishing GSM1k would recreate the contamination it measures, hence the withheld set.
placement_reason: Born to answer whether a public GSM8k score reflects real math reasoning or memorization of the released test set, GSM1k builds a private difficulty-matched twin and reads the accuracy gap as contamination — a contamination-forensics instrument.
one_line: Private, difficulty-matched, human-written twin of GSM8k exposes benchmark overfitting: worst families drop up to 8 points, frontier models flat.
key_number: Worst overfit: Yi-6B-Chat drops 8.0 points (43.7% GSM8k → 35.7% GSM1k); frontier flat (GPT-4o 93.1 → 92.9).

title: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-model use is stated; the three attribution protocols are benchmarked against ground truth, not deployed as a training signal, and the paper's own headline is that they are not yet reliable enough to trust.
placement_reason: Tests whether automated LLM-judge protocols can correctly perform a specific diagnostic judgment (name the responsible agent and decisive step) against human-adjudicated ground truth, finding several method/condition cells score at or below random — the same audit-a-judge's-accuracy structure as JudgeBench/RewardBench, just applied to failure-attribution judgment instead of preference judgment; its own critique flags no formal inter-annotator agreement statistic for the ground truth labels and a same-model-family blind spot (GPT-4o both generates and mostly judges the failures), which is exactly F2's territory rather than V2's rubric-construction spirit, since the paper's contribution is exposing judge unreliability, not shipping a validated grading instrument.
one_line: Formalizes automated failure attribution via a counterfactual "decisive error" definition and ships Who&When, 184 human-adjudicated failure logs across 127 systems; the best of three LLM-judge attribution protocols reaches only 53.5% agent-level and 14.2% step-level accuracy.
key_number: 5 of 12 step-level method/condition cells and 1 of 12 agent-level cells fall below the paper's own random baseline (e.g. All-at-Once averages 8.70% step-level accuracy against an 11.61% random floor).

title: LLM Novice Uplift on Dual-Use, In Silico Biology Tasks
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-model use is stated; the odds-ratio uplift measurement is a red-team-style diagnostic of realistic human-AI misuse risk, not a training signal, and the paper's own critique flags the 89.6% safeguard figure as an absence-of-expressed-difficulty proxy rather than a measured jailbreak rate.
placement_reason: Asks whether dangerous biological capability can be recovered not by a model alone but by a sustained, multi-model human-AI collaboration — the same "can the excluded/gated skill be recovered" question as wei-2025-bioriskeval, extended from a single model's representations to a realistic hours-long uplift protocol with human subjects; a dangerous-capability-recovery probe rather than a one-shot knowledge benchmark, which the paper itself argues under-measures this risk.
one_line: 57 biology novices given up to 13 hours with a fleet of frontier models (o3, o4-mini, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4) score 4.16x higher on eight biosecurity benchmarks than an internet-only control, beating human experts on three of four benchmarks with expert data.
key_number: 89.6% of Treatment participants gave no indication of any difficulty getting dual-use information past model safeguards; but the "beats experts" comparison pits 1.5-13 hours plus a model fleet against unaided experts capped at 15-30 minutes, and standalone LLMs usually outscored the LLM-assisted humans on structured tasks.

title: Calibrate Before Use: Improving Few-Shot Performance of Language Models
reward_readiness_reason: Contextual calibration is a test-time correction applied to a completed forward pass, not a training loss or reward signal — no RL/fine-tuning use is stated anywhere in the paper.
placement_reason: Born to show that a reported few-shot accuracy number is largely an artifact of prompt example order/selection/format rather than a stable measure of task capability (GPT-3 2.7B swings 54.3%→93.4% on identical SST-2 examples merely reordered) and hands back a training-free calibration correction — the same show-a-metric-measures-the-wrong-thing F3 move as sacreBLEU/Emergent Mirage, here aimed at the few-shot evaluation protocol itself.
one_line: GPT-3's few-shot accuracy swings from near-chance to near-state-of-the-art on nothing but example order; three measurable output-distribution biases explain it, corrected with a zero-label, content-free-probe calibration step.
key_number: Calibration lifts accuracy by up to +30.0 points absolute and lets GPT-3 2.7B beat the uncalibrated 175B baseline by up to 19.3 points — but by the paper's own Table 1, it narrows rather than eliminates the sensitivity.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
reward_readiness_reason: Not a reward in-paper, but LLM-judge preference grading became the downstream RLAIF reward paradigm, and the verbosity/self-enhancement biases it quantified are exactly the hacks later rubric-RL reward work (Online Rubrics, Rubric Reward Hacking) fights.
placement_reason: Born to answer "can a strong LLM stand in for costly human preference judging of open-ended multi-turn chat?" — it defines the LLM-as-a-judge protocol and validates it against Arena human votes, the canonical P2 judge-protocol move.
one_line: GPT-4 grading chat answers matches expert human preference 85% (humans agree 81%), turning LLM-as-a-judge into the field's default verdict machine.
key_number: 85% GPT-4-human agreement on non-tie MT-bench votes (vs 81% human-human)

title: Instruction-Following Evaluation for Large Language Models
reward_readiness_reason: Explainer states IFEval "has since become a standard training target, not just an eval" and sits "in many post-training mixes"; deterministic verifiers are free per-verdict → drop-in RLVR reward.
placement_reason: Built to make instruction-following correctness mechanical by restricting the test set to atomic directives a short deterministic program can label followed/not, removing humans and LLM judges from the verdict path.
one_line: Restrict the test set to mechanically-checkable instructions so deterministic programs, not humans or LLM judges, score instruction-following reproducibly.
key_number: 541 prompts covering 25 verifiable instruction types organized into 9 groups; GPT-4 (Nov 2023) 76.89% prompt-level strict

title: SOTOPIA: Interactive Evaluation for Social Intelligence in Language Agents
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/training-signal use in the paper; SOTOPIA-EVAL is reported as a benchmark score for comparing agent social intelligence, and the paper's own critique flags GPT-4-judge self-preference bias rather than any optimization-against-eval use.
placement_reason: Born to answer ‘what does an LLM agent actually do when handed a private, possibly conflicting social goal inside a live multi-turn interaction?’ — replacing static social-intelligence QA with a staged, goal-driven scenario graded on a broad multi-axis behavioral rubric (GOAL/BEL/KNO/REL/FIN/SOC/SEC), the same broad-panel capability-audit pattern as GDPval/Med-PaLM rather than a narrower honesty, danger, or adversarial probe.
one_line: Two LLM agents pursue private, possibly conflicting social goals across up to 20 turns in one of 450 scripted scenarios, scored on seven axes (SOTOPIA-EVAL) instead of one accuracy number; every model still averages negative on norm-following even as GPT-4 leads every dimension.
key_number: GPT-4 leads GOAL 7.62 vs GPT-3.5's 6.45 and Llama-2-70b-chat's 5.38, but SOC/SEC stay negative for all four models (GPT-4: −0.07/−0.14) and human-model agreement is only moderate (Randolph's κ=0.503)

title: DyVal: Dynamic Evaluation of Large Language Models for Reasoning Tasks
reward_readiness_reason: The paper explicitly fine-tunes Llama2-13B-chat (via LoRA) on DyVal-generated data and shows it improves accuracy on 6 existing benchmarks completely disjoint from DyVal's own tasks — dynamically-generated, complexity-controlled problems used directly as a training signal, not just a read-only diagnostic.
placement_reason: Born to answer whether a benchmark can escape both data contamination and fixed-complexity staleness by generating fresh, complexity-controlled reasoning problems on the fly from directed acyclic graphs rather than drawing from a static test set — the same contamination-defense-by-construction move as GSM1k/LiveCodeBench, achieved through dynamic generation with a proven low collision probability (~10^-15) rather than a private holdout or release-date filter.
one_line: Generates reasoning problems on the fly from directed acyclic graphs, with complexity controlled directly by graph depth/width, so no fixed test set exists to memorize (proven collision probability ~10^-15); four of eight tested LLMs score 0% on every task despite strong results on the static benchmarks they were tuned against, and DyVal-generated data used as fine-tuning data improves 6 disjoint existing benchmarks.
key_number: GPT-3.5-Turbo's arithmetic accuracy averages 97.3% at complexity D1 and falls to 71.5% at D4; three models (phi-1.5, WizardMath-13B, Xwin-13B) score exactly 0% on every DyVal task despite reporting strong numbers on their own tuned static benchmarks

title: Where LLM Agents Fail and How They can Learn From Failures
reward_readiness_reason: No RL/reward-model use is stated; AgentErrorBench is a labeled diagnostic dataset for benchmarking detectors, and AgentDebug's own recovery loop is an inference-time debugging technique, not a training reward.
placement_reason: Decomposes "why did this trajectory fail" into a validated, module-and-error-type rubric (17 leaves across 5 modules) scored against human ground truth by Step/Module/ErrorType accuracy — the same failure-diagnosis rubric-verification pattern as MAST, extended with a working recovery loop; placed in V2 rather than F2 because its headline framing is a constructive diagnostic instrument with a reported agreement statistic (κ=0.55), not an audit built to expose judge unreliability.
one_line: A five-module, 17-type failure taxonomy plus AgentErrorBench (200 human-annotated failure trajectories from ALFWorld/GAIA/WebShop, κ=0.55) feeds AgentDebug, which localizes one root-cause step and coaches the agent to a corrected re-rollout.
key_number: AgentDebug reaches 45.0% Step / 31.3% Step+Module / 24.3% All-Correct detection accuracy against home-built baselines topping out at 28.0%/10.0%/0.3% — though its own algorithm box and method prose describe the critical-error-detection mechanism two contradictory ways (LLM-only vs. counterfactual rollout).

title: Establishing Best Practices for Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
reward_readiness_reason: ABC is a 43-item benchmark-construction audit checklist applied/reported to harden graders, not an instrument whose validity depends on not-training-against-it; its warning is that AGENTS game weak graders, which is an eval-design caution, so it is diagnostic-only (unlike the true contamination detectors han-2025/zhang-2024).
placement_reason: Born to ask whether agentic benchmarks' headline numbers are lying — a 43-item rigor checklist plus exploit experiments that audit ten benchmarks — squarely a benchmark-rigor standard, the agentic sibling of ABC-Checklist.
one_line: A 43-check audit checklist for agentic benchmarks — task validity, outcome validity, reporting — under which all ten popular benchmarks examined fail somewhere.
key_number: A do-nothing agent returning an empty response scores 38% on τ-bench-Airline, beating a real GPT-4o-based agent.

title: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents
reward_readiness_reason: Digest: per-requirement DAG verdicts pitched as "a promising reward-signal prototype for agent self-improvement" — dense milestone feedback, though "not yet a settled measurement instrument" and Goodharting risk noted.
placement_reason: Built to make agentic-development correctness mechanically checkable by having an agentic judge verdict each node of a human-authored requirements DAG rather than a single final pass/fail, so it is a rubric-verification harness.
one_line: An agentic judge that opens the workspace and verdicts each requirement in a DAG, matching a single human ~90% at ~2% of cost.
key_number: 90.44% alignment with human consensus judging OpenHands, edging past the best single human (89.89%) at $30.58 vs the panel's $1,297.50 (2.29% of cost)
